Paul pairs creation (calling the nonexistent) with resurrection (giving life to the dead) as twin marks of the God Abraham believed.

echoes.text: I beseech you, my child, to lift your eyes to the heaven and the earth, and to see all things that are therein, and thus to recognize that God made them not of things that were, and that the race of men in this wise comes into being.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) has its closest Second Temple parallel in 2 Maccabees 7:28, where the mother urges her son to recognize 'that God did not make them out of things that existed' — an early articulation of creation from nothing, paired (as in Romans 4) with resurrection hope. Contested background echo.

echoes.text: Yes, my hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand has spread out the heavens: when I call to them, they stand up together.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) may echo the Isaianic creator who 'calls' the heavens and earth into existence (Isaiah 48:13; 41:4; 44:24), where divine calling is creative summons. Faint verbal link via the verb 'call'; marked contested.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: The pericope closes in 4:22 by re-quoting the governing text: 'Therefore it also was reckoned to him for righteousness.' Recurrence of Genesis 15:6 as the inclusio binding the demonstration of Abraham's faith back to its scriptural anchor.

pericopes.text: Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus, our Lord, from the dead, who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted' (4:23-24) explicitly thematizes the act of reading Genesis 15:6 as Scripture written for the church. The verb 'accounted/reckoned' is carried forward one last time, applied now to believers in the God who raised Jesus.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'Who was delivered up for our trespasses' (4:25) echoes Isaiah 53 LXX, especially 53:6 ('the Lord delivered him up for our sins,' paredoken auton tais hamartiais hemon) and 53:12 ('he was delivered up because of their sins'). Paul's verb 'delivered up' (paredothe) plus 'for our trespasses' is verbatim Servant-song language, identifying the crucified Jesus as the suffering Servant.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'And was raised for our justification' (4:25) draws on Isaiah 53:11 LXX, 'the righteous one will justify the many (dikaiosai dikaion... tois pollois), and he shall bear their sins.' The pairing of the Servant's vindication with the justification 'of many' undergirds Paul's resurrection-justification clause, linking the Abraham-righteousness midrash to the Servant's righteousness.

pericopes.text: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering works perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope: and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us. For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a righteous person someone would even dare to die. But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life. Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: "Justified by faith" (5:1) is the conclusion Paul has just drawn from Abraham (Romans 4), and ultimately rests on Genesis 15:6, "Abram believed the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." The faith-righteousness link governing 5:1 is verbally and conceptually the Genesis 15:6 logic carried forward into this pericope's opening clause.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: "The righteous shall live by faith" is Paul's thesis text (Romans 1:17) and stands behind "being justified by faith" (5:1). The faith-life pairing of Habakkuk 2:4 resonates in the move from justification by faith to being "saved by his life" (5:10), though no verbal quotation appears here.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: "Peace with God" (5:1) and reconciliation through Christ's death (5:10-11) echo the Suffering Servant whose "chastisement brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed." Isaiah 53 supplies the template of one man's death securing peace and healing for the many that drives the whole passage.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: "While we were yet sinners/ungodly" Christ died for us (5:6, 5:8): "All we like sheep have gone astray... and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all." The Servant bearing the iniquity of the straying matches Paul's "Christ died for the ungodly."

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: "He poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many" stands behind "Christ died for us" while sinners (5:8) and "justified by his blood" (5:9). The Servant's vicarious death for "many" anticipates the many/one structure Paul develops.

echoes.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
echoes.note: "Justified by his blood" (5:9): "the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement." Paul's atoning-blood language draws on the Levitical principle that blood effects expiation, already invoked at Romans 3:25 (hilasterion).

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: "Justified by his blood" (5:9) may faintly recall the blood of the covenant Moses dashed on the people, sealing the relationship with God. Disputed as a deliberate echo here versus general sacrificial background.

echoes.text: But let all those who take refuge in you rejoice, Let them always shout for joy, because you defend them. Let them also who love your name be joyful in you.
echoes.note: "We rejoice in hope of the glory of God" and "rejoice in God" (5:2, 5:11): "let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy... let those who love your name exult in you." The pattern of those justified/sheltered by God rejoicing/exulting in him is a recurrent Psalmic posture Paul takes up.

echoes.text: They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed.
echoes.note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "they trusted in you and were not put to shame." The Psalmic confession that trust in God does not end in shame is the verbal-conceptual root of Paul's claim that hope ou kataischynei.

echoes.text: Yes, no one who waits for you shall be shamed. They shall be shamed who deal treacherously without cause.
echoes.note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "none who wait for you shall be put to shame." Psalm 25 (vv. 3, 20) repeatedly grounds the assurance that hope in God is not disappointed, matching Paul's claim about hope.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "whoever believes will not be put to shame" (LXX). Paul quotes this very verse at Romans 9:33 and 10:11; the same shame/faith formula colors his statement here that hope does not disappoint.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: "God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (5:5): "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh." The verb "pour out" (ekcheo) applied to the Spirit is the prophetic eschatological-outpouring idiom; Paul quotes Joel 2:32 at Romans 10:13, showing the passage is in view.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: "God's love poured out... through the Holy Spirit" (5:5): "I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring." The same Spirit-outpouring promise, paired with water/blessing imagery, undergirds Paul's image of love flooding the heart by the Spirit.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: "Poured out into our hearts... the Holy Spirit who was given to us" (5:5): "I will give you a new heart... I will put my Spirit within you." The new-covenant promise of God's Spirit placed within the heart matches Paul's interiorized gift of the Spirit and love.

echoes.text: My son, if you come to serve the Lord, Prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, And make not haste in time of calamity. Cleave to him, and depart not, That you may be increased at your latter end. Accept whatever is brought upon you, And be longsuffering when you passest into humiliation. For gold is tried in the fire, And acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.
echoes.note: "Suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance proven character" (5:3-4): "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing... for gold is tested in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation." A Second Temple wisdom commonplace that trials refine and prove the faithful, closely parallel to Paul's chain suffering->endurance->proven character.

echoes.text: And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, And as a whole burnt offering he accepted them.
echoes.note: "Suffering works perseverance... proven character; and proven character, hope" (5:3-4): "Having been disciplined a little, they will receive great good, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself; like gold in the furnace he tried them." Second Temple parallel linking testing/discipline to being proven worthy and to hope of glory (cf. Wisdom 3:4, hope full of immortality).

echoes.text: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.
echoes.note: "Peace with God" through righteousness (5:1): "the work of righteousness shall be peace." The prophetic linkage of righteousness and peace faintly underlies Paul's pairing of justification with peace, though no verbal borrowing is evident.

echoes.text: I will hear what God, Yahweh, will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, his saints; but let them not turn again to folly. Surely his salvation is near those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land. Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
echoes.note: "Peace with God" (5:1): "righteousness and peace kiss each other." The Psalm's union of righteousness and peace as God's salvific gift resonates faintly with Paul's justification-yields-peace claim. Disputed as a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: "Peace with God" for the reconciled (5:1, 5:10-11): "Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the LORD; and I will heal him." The prophetic announcement of peace and healing to estranged people faintly anticipates peace and reconciliation language. Contested.

pericopes.text: Therefore as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; and so death passed to all men, because all sinned. For until the law, sin was in the world; but sin is not charged when there is no law. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those whose sins weren’t like Adam’s disobedience, who is a foreshadowing of him who was to come. But the free gift isn’t like the trespass. For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God, and the gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many. The gift is not as through one who sinned: for the judgment came by one to condemnation, but the free gift came of many trespasses to justification. For if by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one; so much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ. So then as through one trespass, all men were condemned; even so through one act of righteousness, all men were justified to life. For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous. The law came in besides, that the trespass might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly; that as sin reigned in death, even so grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: "Sin entered into the world through one man" (5:12) figurally reads the Eden narrative: Adam's single transgression in eating the forbidden fruit is the entry point of sin into the cosmos. Paul explicitly types Adam as "a foreshadowing of him who was to come" (5:14, typos), making the fall the controlling figure for the Adam-Christ antithesis.

echoes.text: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
echoes.note: "Death through sin... death passed to all" (5:12): "in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." The divine sentence binding death to the one prohibited act is the textual basis for Paul's claim that death entered through the one man's transgression.

echoes.text: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, […]
echoes.note: "Death passed to all men" and "death reigned" (5:12, 5:14, 5:17): "cursed is the ground because of you... you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Adam's curse universalizing death is figurally taken up as the reign of death over all humanity that Christ's act of righteousness reverses.

echoes.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
echoes.note: "Through the one man's disobedience many were made sinners" (5:19): "she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband, and he ate." Adam's specific act of disobedient eating is the trespass/parakoe Paul opposes to Christ's obedience (hypakoe).

echoes.text: God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
echoes.note: "Adam's disobedience" / "the one man's disobedience" (5:14, 5:19): "Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" God's interrogation frames Adam's act precisely as disobedience to a command, supplying the parakoe Paul contrasts with Christ's obedience.

echoes.text: Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he became the father of other sons and daughters. All the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, then he died. Seth lived one hundred five years, then became the father of Enosh. Seth lived after he became the father of Enosh eight […]
echoes.note: "Death reigned from Adam until Moses" (5:14): the tolling refrain "and he died" through the Sethite genealogy (Genesis 5) concretizes the unbroken reign of death over the generations between Adam and the giving of the law. Paul's historical span presupposes this litany of mortality.

echoes.text: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being; But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.
echoes.note: "Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin" (5:12): "God created man for incorruption... but through the devil's envy death entered the world." The closest Second Temple parallel, sharing the precise idiom "death entered the world" (eiselthen... thanatos) and tracing universal death to a primeval cause. Paul localizes the cause in Adam's trespass rather than the devil's envy.

echoes.text: From a woman was the beginning of sin; And because of her we all die.
echoes.note: "Through one... death" passed to all (5:12, 5:15): "From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die." A Second Temple text tracing universal death to the primeval transgression in Eden, structurally parallel to Paul (though Ben Sira blames Eve, Paul Adam). Strong thematic overlap on death-through-one.

echoes.text: God spoke all these words, saying, “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the […]
echoes.note: "Death reigned from Adam until Moses" and "the law came in besides" (5:14, 5:20): the Sinai law-giving through Moses is the temporal boundary and the "law that came in" so that the trespass might increase. Paul presupposes the Mosaic legislation (Exodus 20 / the Decalogue) as the entry of nomos into his salvation-history scheme.

echoes.text: Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
echoes.note: "Grace... reign through righteousness to eternal life" (5:21): the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24), forfeited at the fall, faintly stands behind the restoration of "eternal life" through the second Adam. A disputed figural undertone rather than a verbal echo.

echoes.text: But they, like Adam, have broken the covenant. They were unfaithful to me, there.
echoes.note: "As through one trespass... all condemned" (5:18): "like Adam they transgressed the covenant" (one reading of Hosea 6:7) treats Adam as the archetypal covenant-breaker. A faint and textually disputed possible precedent for Paul's Adam-as-transgressor typology.

pericopes.text: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer? Or don’t you know that all we who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him through baptism to death, that just like Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection; knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin. For he who has died has been freed from sin. But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him; knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no more has dominion over him! For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God. Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Neither present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God, as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The valley of dry bones: God brings the dead up from their graves to new life by his Spirit. Paul's death-and-burial-then-'newness of life' (6:4) and 'alive from the dead' (6:13) share the figural movement of resurrection-as-new-existence, though Paul grounds it christologically rather than nationally.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: New heart and new spirit enabling obedience; 'newness of life' (6:4, kainotes zoes) coheres with the prophetic promise of interior renewal. Faint and disputed verbal contact, but the renewal/new-walk theme is shared.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A type of death-and-resurrection-to-life that early Christian reading connected to Christ's raising; resonates with 6:4-5,8-9 union in death and resurrection. Faint and contested.

pericopes.text: What then? Shall we sin, because we are not under law, but under grace? May it never be! Don’t you know that to whom you present yourselves as servants to obedience, his servants you are whom you obey; whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness? But thanks be to God, that, whereas you were bondservants of sin, you became obedient from the heart to that form of teaching to which you were delivered. Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness. I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh, for as you presented your members as servants to uncleanness and to wickedness upon wickedness, even so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification. For when you were servants of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, being made free from sin, and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification, and the result of eternal life. For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

echoes.text: For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves.
echoes.note: 'For they are my servants (slaves), whom I brought out of the land of Egypt' (cf. 25:55). The structural logic of 6:16-22 - one cannot be masterless; freed from one slavery you become a slave of another, and God's people are rightly God's slaves - mirrors the exodus principle that liberation from Pharaoh = transfer to YHWH's service. Coheres with Paul's 'made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness/God.'

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: The two ways: 'I have set before you life and death... therefore choose life.' Romans 6:21-23 frames the alternatives as 'the end of those things is death' versus 'eternal life,' the same life-or-death covenantal antithesis. Thematic coherence is high even without verbatim borrowing.

echoes.text: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
echoes.note: 'In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die' - sin's penalty is death. 'The wages of sin is death' (6:23) restates the Edenic verdict that disobedience earns death. A foundational thematic echo behind the whole sin-death nexus of 5-6.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: 'You shall return to the ground... to dust you shall return' - death as the consequence of the fall. With 'wages of sin is death' (6:23) and 'the end of those things is death' (6:21) Paul echoes the Genesis sentence; note also 'the things of which you are now ashamed' (6:21) resonating with the shame of Genesis 3:7-10.

echoes.text: Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins, he shall die.
echoes.note: 'The soul that sins shall die' (cf. 18:20). A near-proverbial scriptural maxim that sin yields death, closely cohering with 'the wages of sin is death' (6:23). Strong thematic, no formula.

echoes.text: It shall be, if he tells you, “I will not go out from you,” because he loves you and your house, because he is well with you; then you shall take an awl, and thrust it through his ear to the door, and he shall be your servant forever. Also to your female servant you shall do likewise.
echoes.note: The bondservant who loves his master may give himself permanently into service 'because he is well off with you' (cf. Exodus 21:5-6, serving 'forever'). Paul's voluntary, glad slavery 'obedient from the heart' (6:17) and willingly becoming 'bondservants of righteousness' (6:18) reflects this paradox of chosen, heartfelt servitude. Faint and disputed.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: Circumcision of the heart so that you love and obey God; 'obedient from the heart' (6:17) echoes the prophetic-Deuteronomic ideal of interior, not merely external, obedience. Faint.

echoes.text: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'Choose this day whom you will serve' - the demand to declare allegiance to one master. Coheres with 6:16's binary of presenting oneself as slave to sin-unto-death or to obedience-unto-righteousness. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt' - the resurrection antithesis of life vs. shameful death. 'Eternal life' (6:22-23) over against death, with shame in 6:21, coheres with this Second-Temple resurrection hope. Faint and disputed.

echoes.text: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being; But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.
echoes.note: Deuterocanonical: 'God created man for incorruption... but through the devil's envy death entered the world' (cf. 1:13, 'God did not make death'). A Second-Temple articulation that death is the intruding wage of sin, thematically close to 'the wages of sin is death' (6:23). Contested.

echoes.text: Say not you, It is through the Lord that I fell away; For you shall not do the things that he hates. Say not you, It is he that caused me to err; For he has no need of a sinful man. The Lord hates every abomination; And those who fear him love it not. He himself made man from the beginning, And left him in the hand of his own counsel. If you will, you shall keep the commandments; And to perform faithfulness is of your own good pleasure. He has set fire […]
echoes.note: Deuterocanonical: 'Before a man are life and death, and whichever he chooses will be given to him'; sin and its death-penalty are laid on human choice. Coheres with the choose-your-master / death-or-life structure of 6:16,21-23. Faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Or don’t you know, brothers (for I speak to men who know the law), that the law has dominion over a man for as long as he lives? For the woman that has a husband is bound by law to the husband while he lives, but if the husband dies, she is discharged from the law of the husband. So then if, while the husband lives, she is joined to another man, she would be called an adulteress. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is no adulteress, though she is joined to another man. Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God. For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were through the law, worked in our members to bring out fruit to death. But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were held; so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them: ‘If any man’s wife goes astray, and is unfaithful to him, and a man lies with her carnally, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and is kept close, and she is defiled, and there is no witness against her, and she isn’t taken in the act; and the spirit of jealousy comes on him, and he is jealous of his wife, and she is defiled: or if the spirit of jealousy comes on […]
echoes.note: Paul's marriage analogy—wife bound to husband, adulteress if joined to another while he lives—draws on the Torah's marriage/adultery law world; the suspected-adultery ordeal is the closest legal backdrop for a wife 'called an adulteress' (7:3).

echoes.text: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter […]
echoes.note: The release of a woman from the 'law of the husband' by death (7:2-3) trades on Torah marriage/divorce regulation; Deuteronomy 24 frames the legal binding and loosing of a wife that Paul presupposes.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: The picture of a woman 'joined to' (lit. 'becoming another man's') stands behind 7:3-4's language of being 'joined to another'; the one-flesh union of Genesis supplies the marital frame Paul figuratively repurposes for union with the risen Christ.

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: The charge 'she would be called an adulteress' (7:3) presupposes the seventh commandment's prohibition of adultery as the legal norm making the analogy intelligible.

pericopes.text: What shall we say then? Is the law sin? May it never be! However, I wouldn’t have known sin, except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting, unless the law had said, “You shall not covet.” But sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting. For apart from the law, sin is dead. I was alive apart from the law once, but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. The commandment, which was for life, this I found to be for death; for sin, finding occasion through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me. Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and righteous, and good.

echoes.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: Direct verbatim citation: 'You shall not covet' (7:7) quotes the tenth commandment of the Decalogue, the LXX 'ouk epithymeseis,' which Paul makes the test case for the law's relation to sin.

echoes.text: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. Neither shall you desire your neighbor’s house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: The Decalogue's second giving repeats 'You shall not covet'; Paul's citation (7:7) matches both forms. Deuteronomy's expanded list ('your neighbor's wife... house... field') makes coveting the representative inward sin Paul exploits.

echoes.text: Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”
echoes.note: 'Sin... deceived me, and through it killed me' (7:11) strongly echoes Eve's 'the serpent deceived me' (LXX 'exepatesen me'); Paul uses the same verb (exapatao), casting sin in the serpent's role of beguiling and bringing death.

echoes.text: Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
echoes.note: 'I was alive apart from the law once, but when the commandment came... I died' (7:9-10) re-enacts Adam in Eden: a single commandment given for life that, transgressed, brings death—the 'I' figurally personates Adam under the one prohibition.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: The whole drama of 7:7-11—commandment, sin seizing opportunity, desire aroused, deception, death—maps onto the Fall narrative: the serpent's exploitation of the prohibition to provoke desire and bring death.

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The commandment, which was for life' (7:10) alludes to the Torah promise that the one who does the statutes 'shall live by them'; Paul cites Leviticus 18:5 explicitly elsewhere (Rom 10:5; Gal 3:12), confirming this as the 'life' the commandment promised.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: The law set before Israel 'life and death,' commanding obedience 'that you may live'; this Deuteronomic life-or-death framing of the commandment underlies Paul's 'the commandment which was for life... I found to be for death' (7:10).

echoes.text: The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
echoes.note: Sin 'finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting' (7:8) echoes the serpent's strategy of turning the prohibition into the very lever of illicit desire ('you will be like God').

echoes.text: But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.
echoes.note: 'Through the devil's envy death entered the world' supplies the Second Temple reading of Genesis 3 that Paul presupposes—personified agency (sin/devil) bringing death through the primal commandment, behind 7:8-11.

echoes.text: From a woman was the beginning of sin; And because of her we all die.
echoes.note: 'From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die' is the Ben Sira tradition linking the Eden transgression to death; it stands in the background of Paul's sin-came-alive-and-I-died account (7:9-11).

echoes.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
echoes.note: Eve seeing the tree 'a delight (epithymeton) to the eyes' couples desire/coveting with the first transgression; Paul's choice of coveting (epithymia) as the paradigm sin (7:7-8) resonates with this Edenic desire.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s testimony is sure, making wise the simple. Yahweh’s precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. Yahweh’s commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes.
echoes.note: 'The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and righteous, and good' (7:12) echoes the psalm's praise of the law as perfect, right, and pure—the OT confession of Torah's goodness that Paul reaffirms.

echoes.text: Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness. Your law is truth.
echoes.note: 'Your law is truth' and the psalm's sustained praise of the commandments as righteous and good lie behind Paul's vindication of the commandment as 'holy and righteous and good' (7:12).

echoes.text: “You came down also on Mount Sinai, and spoke with them from heaven, and gave them right ordinances and true laws, good statutes and commandments,
echoes.note: Israel's confession that God gave 'right ordinances and true laws, good statutes and commandments' parallels Paul's catalogue of the commandment as 'holy, righteous, and good' (7:12).

echoes.text: And it is not merely the stimulus of sensual indulgence, but that of every desire, that reasoning is able to master. For instance, the law says, You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor. Now, then, since it is the law which has forbidden us to desire, I shall much the more easily persuade you, that reasoning is able to govern our lusts, just as it does the affections which are impediments to justice.
echoes.note: 4 Maccabees singles out the law's command against coveting/desire as the test of reason mastering the passions; this Second Temple reflection on 'You shall not covet' as the inward law of desire parallels Paul's use of the same commandment (7:7-8).

pericopes.text: Did then that which is good become death to me? May it never be! But sin, that it might be shown to be sin, by working death to me through that which is good; that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful. For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am fleshly, sold under sin. For I don’t know what I am doing. For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do. But if what I don’t desire, that I do, I consent to the law that it is good. So now it is no more I that do it, but sin which dwells in me. For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice. But if what I don’t desire, that I do, it is no more I that do it, but sin which dwells in me. I find then the law, that, to me, while I desire to do good, evil is present. For I delight in God’s law after the inward man, but I see a different law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin which is in my members. What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord! So then with the mind, I myself serve God’s law, but with the flesh, the sin’s law.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: 'In my flesh dwells no good thing' (7:18) resonates with the antediluvian verdict that 'every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil continually'—the OT root of the doctrine of indwelling evil impulse.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: 'The inclination (yetser) of the human heart is evil from youth' is the scriptural seed of the rabbinic evil-impulse doctrine that frames Paul's 'sin which dwells in me' and the divided will (7:17-20).

echoes.text: Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin my mother conceived me.
echoes.note: 'I am fleshly, sold under sin' (7:14) echoes the penitential confession of being conceived in iniquity—a self caught in sin from the inside, unable to free itself.

echoes.text: Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do that which is evil in the sight of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Sold under sin' (7:14) uses the idiom of being 'sold to do evil,' as Ahab 'sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD'; the same selling-into-bondage metaphor for moral captivity.

echoes.text: but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
echoes.note: 'I delight in God's law after the inward man' (7:22) echoes the blessed one whose 'delight is in the law of the LORD'; Paul affirms the psalmist's delight even as he reports its frustration by the flesh.

echoes.text: I will delight myself in your statutes. I will not forget your word.
echoes.note: The psalmist's repeated delight in God's statutes ('I will delight in your statutes,' 'Oh how I love your law') stands behind 7:22's 'I delight in God's law after the inward man.'

echoes.text: How I love your law! It is my meditation all day.
echoes.note: 'Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day' is the paradigmatic Torah-delight Paul invokes for the inner self that consents to the law as good (7:22, 7:16).

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promised circumcision of the heart so as to love God is the inward-law hope behind Paul's 'inward man' delighting in God's law (7:22), even as he laments its present captivity.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant promise of the law written on the heart underlies the tension Paul dramatizes between the law of the mind/inward man and the law in the members (7:22-23)—the heart that delights versus the flesh that resists.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: Sin 'crouching at the door' whose desire is for Cain, which he must master, prefigures Paul's sin 'dwelling in me' and warring to bring captivity (7:17, 7:23)—personified sin contending for mastery over the self.

echoes.text: For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, And the earthy frame lies heavy on a mind that is full of cares.
echoes.note: 'A perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the thoughtful mind' is the closest Second Temple parallel to Paul's body/mind conflict and 'the body of this death' (7:23-24).

echoes.text: I am pained and bowed down greatly. I go mourning all day long. For my waist is filled with burning. There is no soundness in my flesh. I am faint and severely bruised. I have groaned by reason of the anguish of my heart.
echoes.note: The psalmist's groaning 'wretched' lament under the weight of his own sin parallels Paul's cry 'What a wretched man I am!' (7:24)—the OT idiom of self-directed misery awaiting deliverance.

echoes.text: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name. The righteous will surround me, for you will be good to me.
echoes.note: 'Bring my soul out of prison' voices the deliverance plea that shapes Paul's 'Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?' (7:24)—captivity language answered by rescue.

echoes.text: The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: 'The cords of death... the pangs of Sheol... then I called on the name of the LORD: O LORD, deliver my soul' parallels the wretched-self-to-deliverance movement of 7:24-25.

echoes.text: And I answered and said, O you earth, wherefore have you brought forth, if the mind is made out of dust, like as all other created things? For it were better that the dust itself had been unborn, so that the mind might not have been made therefrom. But now the mind grows with us, and by reason of this we are tormented, because we perish and know it. Let the race of men lament and the beasts of the field be glad; let all that are born lament, but let the […]
echoes.note: 4 Ezra's lament over the 'evil heart' (cor malignum) that burdens humanity and frustrates the good is the nearest Second Temple analogue to Paul's anatomy of the divided self enslaved by indwelling sin (7:14-24).

pericopes.text: There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death. For what the law couldn’t do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh; that the ordinance of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace; because the mind of the flesh is hostile towards God; for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be. Those who are in the flesh can’t please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if it is so that the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if any man doesn’t have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you. So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh. For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God. For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ; if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.

echoes.text: if the anointed priest sins so as to bring guilt on the people, then let him offer for his sin, which he has sinned, a young bull without defect to Yahweh for a sin offering.
echoes.note: 'for sin' (peri hamartias) in v.3 reproduces the Septuagint's standing phrase for the sin offering; God's sending his Son 'for sin' figurally casts Christ in the role of the Levitical purification sacrifice that 'condemns sin in the flesh.'

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The Spirit enabling 'the ordinance of the law' to be 'fulfilled in us' (v.4) draws on the new-covenant promise to write the Torah on the heart, internalizing the law by divine agency rather than external command.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' undergirds vv.4-9: the indwelling Spirit (vv.9,11) produces obedience and 'walking according to the Spirit'; the verbal cluster Spirit-indwelling-walking-statutes is distinctive to Ezekiel.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live' (the dry-bones vision) lies behind v.11, where the Spirit who raised Jesus 'will also give life to your mortal bodies'; Spirit-giving-life-to-dead-bodies is the precise Ezekielian figure.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: The flesh/Spirit antithesis (vv.5-9), where 'flesh' marks mortal humanity opposed to God's enduring Spirit, faintly recalls 'My Spirit will not abide in man forever, for he is flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The spirit is alive' / God giving 'life to your mortal bodies' (vv.10-11) faintly evokes the breath of life animating dust-formed Adam, now reapplied as resurrection-life by the Spirit.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: 'The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace' and 'if you live after the flesh you must die... by the Spirit... you will live' (vv.6,13) reframe the covenantal life-and-death choice of Moses' exhortation set before Israel.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn, and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
echoes.note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' grounds the sonship/adoption language of vv.14-17; the Spirit constitutes believers as 'children of God,' transferring Israel's sonship status to those led by the Spirit.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the adopted-son-led-by-God motif (vv.14-15); the tender father-son relation undergirds the cry 'Abba! Father!'

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, it shall be said, You are children of the living God' anticipates 'these are children of God' / 'we are children of God' (vv.14,16); Paul cites this very text in Romans 9:26.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: 'You, O LORD, are our Father' — Israel's corporate address of God as Father — stands behind the Spirit-prompted filial cry 'Abba! Father!' (v.15).

echoes.text: “But I said, ‘How I would put you among the children, and give you a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the armies of the nations!’ and I said, ‘You shall call me “My Father”, and shall not turn away from following me.’
echoes.note: 'I thought you would call me My Father and would not turn from following me' — God's hope that adopted Israel address him as Father — resonates with the adoptive cry of v.15.

echoes.text: I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: The covenant formula 'I will... be your God, and you shall be my people,' realized through the indwelling Spirit (vv.9-16), faintly underlies the divine-belonging and sonship affirmed by the Spirit's testimony.

pericopes.text: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us. For the creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. For the creation was subjected to vanity, not of its own will, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now. Not only so, but ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body. For we were saved in hope, but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for that which he sees? But if we hope for that which we don’t see, we wait for it with patience. In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered. He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God. We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, to those who are called according to his purpose. For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified.

echoes.text: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, […]
echoes.note: 'The creation was subjected to vanity... in hope' (vv.20-22) directly invokes the curse on the ground 'because of you,' the toil, thorns, and frustrated labor of the fall; creation's bondage to decay is the Edenic curse awaiting reversal.

echoes.text: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
echoes.note: Creation 'subjected to vanity' (mataiotes, v.20) reuses the Septuagint's rendering of hevel ('vanity of vanities'); Qoheleth's diagnosis of the cosmos's futile, breath-like emptiness is the condition from which creation longs for release.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: 'I create new heavens and a new earth' is the hope toward which the groaning creation strains (vv.19-22): the liberation of creation 'into the liberty of the glory of the children of God' is the prophetic new-creation renewal of the cosmos.

echoes.text: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them. The cow and the bear will graze. Their young ones will lie down together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for […]
echoes.note: The peaceable, restored creation under the messianic shoot — wolf with lamb, no harm in all God's holy mountain — anticipates creation 'delivered from the bondage of decay,' the redeemed cosmos liberated alongside God's children (vv.19-21).

echoes.text: The earth mourns and fades away. The world languishes and fades away. The lofty people of the earth languish. The earth also is polluted under its inhabitants, because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, and broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore the curse has devoured the earth, and those who dwell therein are found guilty. Therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left. The new wine mourns. The vine […]
echoes.note: 'The earth mourns and withers... the earth is defiled under its inhabitants' depicts the groaning land suffering under human transgression, parallel to creation subjected to futility and groaning (vv.20-22).

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh. We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.
echoes.note: 'Like a woman with child... we writhed in pain' supplies the birth-pang imagery of 'the whole creation groans and travails in pain together' (v.22); creation labors toward the deliverance of new life.

echoes.text: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she gave birth to her children. Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to be delivered?” says Yahweh: “shall I who cause to give birth shut the womb?” says your God.
echoes.note: Zion's travail bringing forth her children before her pain comes echoes the link between creation's birth-pangs (v.22) and the 'revealing of the children of God' / 'redemption of the body' (vv.19,23).

echoes.text: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.
echoes.note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of judgment and impending deliverance resonates faintly with the cosmic travail of v.22.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' as eschatological down-payment resonates with 'the first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23), the Spirit as the firstfruits/guarantee of the coming redemption.

echoes.text: The first of the first fruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
echoes.note: 'The first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23) draws on the cultic firstfruits offering that consecrates and pledges the full harvest; the Spirit is the consecrating pledge of the redeemed body.

echoes.text: Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord? Arise! Don’t reject us forever. Why do you hide your face, and forget our affliction and our oppression? For our soul is bowed down to the dust. Our body clings to the earth. Rise up to help us. Redeem us for your loving kindness’ sake.
echoes.note: The lament's 'why do you sleep?... our soul is bowed down... redeem us' anticipates the groaning, waiting, and hoped-for redemption (vv.23-25); the same psalm is quoted at v.36.

echoes.text: Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you.
echoes.note: 'All my longing is before you; my groaning is not hidden from you' resonates with the inarticulate groaning the Spirit voices before 'him who searches the hearts' (vv.26-27).

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' undergirds 'he who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit's mind' (v.27); God's heart-discerning gaze validates the wordless intercession.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind' supplies the precise epithet 'he who searches the hearts' (v.27); the heart-searcher reads the Spirit's unutterable groanings.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar.
echoes.note: 'O LORD, you have searched me and known me... you discern my thoughts from afar' resonates with God searching the hearts and knowing the Spirit's mind (v.27).

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: Being 'conformed to the image of his Son' (v.29) reworks humanity's creation in the image of God; the restored image is now christological, the Son as the prototype to which the predestined are refashioned.

echoes.text: I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.
echoes.note: 'I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth' grounds 'that he might be the firstborn among many brothers' (v.29); the Davidic-messianic firstborn title is extended to the Son who heads a redeemed family.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
echoes.note: 'Israel is my firstborn son' reinforces the 'firstborn among many brothers' (v.29): the firstborn-son status, once Israel's, belongs to the Son who incorporates many siblings.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you... I appointed you' supplies the foreknowing-and-appointing pattern of vv.29-30; divine foreknowledge as elective purpose precedes calling.

echoes.text: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name:
echoes.note: The Servant 'called from the womb,' named before birth, resonates with the chain of foreknowing, predestining, and calling in vv.29-30.

echoes.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.
echoes.note: 'You meant evil... but God meant it for good' faintly underlies 'all things work together for good for those who love God' (v.28); divine providence turning suffering toward good.

echoes.text: and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
echoes.note: 'Showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments' supplies the covenantal designation 'those who love God' (v.28), the loving-God-and-being-blessed pattern.

pericopes.text: What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things? Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? Even as it is written, “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.” No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

echoes.text: Yes, for your sake we are killed all day long. We are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.
echoes.note: v.36 cites verbatim with the formula 'even as it is written': 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.' The lament psalm of the righteous suffering for God's sake interprets the believers' affliction (v.35).

echoes.text: He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.
echoes.note: The Servant's courtroom taunt 'He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?... It is the Lord GOD who helps me; who will declare me guilty?' is reworked into 'Who could bring a charge against God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns?' (vv.33-34); the forensic question-and-answer pattern is shared.

echoes.text: He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy, neither do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.”
echoes.note: 'He who didn't spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all' (v.32) echoes the Aqedah, where God says to Abraham 'you have not withheld (spared) your son, your only son'; God now does for all what Abraham was prepared to do, the Father not sparing his own Son.

echoes.text: and said, “I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son,
echoes.note: 'Because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son' reinforces v.32; the Septuagint's verb for 'spare/withhold' (pheidomai) is the same word Paul uses, strengthening the Aqedah allusion.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' and the Servant 'delivered up' (LXX paradidomi, 53:6,12) stands behind 'delivered him up for us all' (v.32); the handing-over of the Servant for the many.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The Servant 'poured out his soul to death... bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors' resonates with Christ who 'makes intercession for us' (v.34); both join self-giving death with ongoing intercession.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Sit at my right hand' grounds 'who is at the right hand of God' (v.34); the enthronement of the exalted Lord secures his advocacy and the impossibility of any condemnation.

echoes.text: Yahweh is on my side. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?' supplies the rhetorical shape of 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); the same God-for-me-therefore-fearless logic.

echoes.text: Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD is with us; do not fear them' resonates with 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); divine presence nullifies opposing power.

echoes.text: Then my enemies shall turn back in the day that I call. I know this, that God is for me.
echoes.note: 'This I know, that God is for me' is a near-verbal antecedent to 'God is for us' (v.31), the confidence that God's siding with the petitioner routs adversaries.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came at me to eat up my flesh, even my adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell. Though an army should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear. Though war should rise against me, even then I will be confident.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?... though war arise against me, yet I will be confident' resonates with the catalogue of perils that cannot prevail (vv.35,37-39).

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'There is no god besides me... I kill and I make alive' underlies the totalizing pairing 'neither death, nor life' (v.38) as the extremes wholly within God's sovereign love.

echoes.text: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in Yahweh. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!
echoes.note: The catalogue of deprivations (failed crops, no flock) followed by 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD' parallels the list of hardships in v.35 that cannot separate from God's love, culminating in triumphant confidence (v.37).

echoes.text: If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.
echoes.note: The three youths' confidence that 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us' amid fire and sword resonates with believers as 'more than conquerors' through perils including 'sword' (vv.35-37).

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]
echoes.note: 'The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them... having been disciplined a little they will receive great good' parallels the assurance that no affliction separates from God's love (vv.35-39); the righteous tested 'like gold in the furnace' and found worthy.

echoes.text: But the righteous live forever, And in the Lord is their reward, And the care for them with the Most High. Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.
echoes.note: 'The righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord... they will receive a glorious crown' resonates with being 'more than conquerors' and inseparable from God's love (vv.37-39).

echoes.text: And it came to pass that seven kindred also with their mother were at the king’s command taken and shamefully handled with scourges and cords, to compel them to taste of the abominable swine’s flesh. But one of them made himself the spokesman and said, What would you ask and learn of us? for we are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers. And the king fell into a rage, and commanded to heat pans and caldrons: and when these forthwith […]
echoes.note: The martyr-mother and seven sons, killed 'all day long' for covenant faithfulness yet confident of resurrection, resonate with 'for your sake we are killed all day long' read as triumphant martyrdom (vv.36-37).

echoes.text: He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither shall you be afraid of destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, neither shall you be afraid of the animals of the earth.
echoes.note: 'In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword' enumerates perils paralleling v.35's famine, sword, and danger, with God's protection through them.

pericopes.text: I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers’ sake, my relatives according to the flesh, who are Israelites; whose is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises; of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh, who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
