echoes.note: Paul's wish in v.3 that he himself were 'accursed (anathema) from Christ' for his kinsmen echoes Moses' intercession after the golden calf: 'blot me out of your book' rather than destroy Israel. Both are intercessors offering self-substitution/self-curse to spare the people; the Exodus 32 setting also frames the whole chapter's mercy-language (33:19 quoted at v.15).

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
echoes.note: The catalogue of Israel's privileges (adoption, glory, covenants, law-giving, service, promises, fathers) in vv.4-5 draws on the Deuteronomic election traditions naming Israel as God's chosen, holy people set above the nations.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
echoes.note: 'Whose is the adoption (huiothesia)' (v.4) recalls the sonship of Israel: 'Israel is my firstborn son.' Israel's national adoption is the OT root of the privilege Paul lists.

echoes.text: As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, Yahweh’s glory appeared in the cloud.
echoes.note: 'The glory' (doxa, v.4) evokes the Shekinah glory of the LORD that appeared to Israel in the wilderness and dwelt in tabernacle/temple — a covenant privilege belonging to Israel.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: 'The covenants' and 'the promises' (vv.4) point to the patriarchal covenant with Abraham and his seed, the seed-theme Paul immediately develops in vv.6-9.

echoes.text: He shows his word to Jacob; his statutes and his ordinances to Israel. He has not done this for just any nation. They don’t know his ordinances. Praise Yah!
echoes.note: 'The giving of the law' (nomothesia) as a unique privilege of Israel echoes the psalm's boast that God 'declares his word to Jacob... He has not dealt so with any nation.'

pericopes.text: But it is not as though the word of God has come to nothing. For they are not all Israel, that are of Israel. Neither, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children. But, “In Isaac will your seed be called.” That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as a seed. For this is a word of promise, “At the appointed time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.” Not only so, but Rebekah also conceived by one, by our father Isaac. For being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls, it was said to her, “The elder will serve the younger.” Even as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

echoes.text: God said to Abraham, “Don’t let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your handmaid. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For from Isaac will your seed be called.
echoes.note: Formula-marked citation in v.7: 'In Isaac will your seed be called' is verbatim from God's word to Abraham concerning Ishmael and Isaac. Paul uses it to prove that physical descent does not equal the elect 'seed' — only the line of promise counts.

echoes.text: He said, “I will certainly return to you when the season comes round. Behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.” Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him.
echoes.note: v.9 'At the appointed time I will come, and Sarah will have a son' explicitly named 'a word of promise.' Conflates the LXX of Genesis 18:10 ('I will return to you at this season') with the promise of a son; the miraculous, promise-born birth of Isaac grounds Paul's 'children of the promise' argument.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to her, “Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be separated from your body. The one people will be stronger than the other people. The elder will serve the younger.”
echoes.note: v.12 'The elder will serve the younger' is verbatim from the oracle to Rebekah about Jacob and Esau in the womb. Paul cites it to show election precedes birth and works ('being not yet born, neither having done good or bad').

echoes.text: “I have loved you,” says Yahweh. Yet you say, “How have you loved us?” “Wasn’t Esau Jacob’s brother?” says Yahweh, “Yet I loved Jacob; but Esau I hated, and made his mountains a desolation, and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.”
echoes.note: v.13 'as it is written, Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' is a formula-cited verbatim quotation of Malachi's oracle, which itself reflects back on the Genesis Jacob/Esau election. Caps the argument that God's elective love is unmerited and prior.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: The 'appointed time' clause of v.9 also echoes Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return... and Sarah shall have a son,' reinforcing that Isaac is born by divine power, not by natural descent.

echoes.text: Isaac entreated Yahweh for his wife, because she was barren. Yahweh was entreated by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
echoes.note: v.10 'Rebekah also conceived by one' alludes to the narrative of Isaac and Rebekah; Paul stresses both twins share one father and one conception to isolate election as the only differentiator.

pericopes.text: What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be! For he said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I caused you to be raised up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” So then, he has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires.

echoes.text: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.”
echoes.note: v.15 'he said to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion' is a verbatim LXX quotation of God's self-revelation to Moses. Grounds divine freedom in mercy and answers the charge of unrighteousness.

echoes.text: but indeed for this cause I have made you stand: to show you my power, and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth;
echoes.note: v.17 'the Scripture says to Pharaoh, For this very purpose I caused you to be raised up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth' is a formula-marked quotation. Pharaoh is the foil to Moses: God's freedom both to show mercy and to harden.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.
echoes.note: v.18 'he hardens whom he desires' draws on the recurring Exodus motif that the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 14:4). Paul generalizes the hardening theme from the plague narrative.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The mercy/compassion pairing of v.15 resonates with the divine-name proclamation that follows in Exodus 34:6, 'merciful and gracious,' the immediate sequel to 33:19 — the same theophanic context Paul mines.

pericopes.text: You will say then to me, “Why does he still find fault? For who withstands his will?” But indeed, O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?” Or hasn’t the potter a right over the clay, from the same lump to make one part a vessel for honor, and another for dishonor? What if God, willing to show his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath made for destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory, us, whom he also called, not from the Jews only, but also from the Gentiles? As he says also in Hosea, “I will call them ‘my people,’ which were not my people; and her ‘beloved,’ who was not beloved.” “It will be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ There they will be called ‘children of the living God.’” Isaiah cries concerning Israel, “If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved; for He will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness, because the LORD will make a short work upon the earth.” As Isaiah has said before, “Unless the Lord of Armies had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

echoes.text: You turn things upside down! Should the potter be thought to be like clay; that the thing made should say about him who made it, “He didn’t make me”; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, “He has no understanding?”
echoes.note: v.20 'Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, Why did you make me like this?' echoes Isaiah's rebuke of the clay that questions the potter, 'Shall the thing made say of him who made it, He did not make me?' Paul's potter/clay rebuttal is built on this prophetic protest-against-protest.

echoes.text: Woe to him who strives with his Maker— a clay pot among the clay pots of the earth! Shall the clay ask him who fashions it, ‘What are you making?’ or your work, ‘He has no hands?’
echoes.note: v.20-21 also draws on Isaiah 45:9, 'Woe to him who strives with his Maker... shall the clay say to him who fashions it, What are you making?' The 'who are you to reply against God' (antapokrinomenos) directly answers Isaiah's woe against the clay that contends with the potter.

echoes.text: House of Israel, can’t I do with you as this potter? says Yahweh. Behold, as the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.
echoes.note: v.21 'has not the potter a right over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?' alludes to Jeremiah's potter's-house oracle: 'as the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.' Supplies the sovereign-potter image and the right to remake.

echoes.text: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”
echoes.note: v.25, formula-marked ('As he says also in Hosea'): 'I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, who was not beloved' quotes Hosea's reversal of Lo-Ammi/Lo-Ruhamah. Paul applies the restoration of unfaithful Israel to the calling of Gentiles.

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: v.26 'in the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, there they will be called children of the living God' is a verbatim quotation of Hosea 1:10 (LXX 2:1), continuing the Lo-Ammi reversal that Paul reads as the inclusion of the Gentiles among God's children.

echoes.text: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, in the midst of all the earth.
echoes.note: v.27-28, formula-marked ('Isaiah cries concerning Israel'): 'If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved; for He will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness' quotes Isaiah's remnant oracle. Establishes the remnant theology central to ch.9-11.

echoes.text: Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah.
echoes.note: v.29, formula-marked ('As Isaiah has said before'): 'Unless the Lord of Armies had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made like Gomorrah' is a verbatim LXX quotation. Reinforces that survival rests entirely on God's gracious preservation of a remnant 'seed.'

echoes.text: Now therefore don’t be scoffers, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, on the whole earth.
echoes.note: The 'finishing/cutting short' decisive-action language of v.28 also draws on Isaiah 28:22, 'a full end, decreed upon the whole earth,' blended with 10:22-23; both stand behind Paul's compressed remnant-judgment formula.

echoes.text: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies.
echoes.note: 'As the sand of the sea' (v.27) verbally re-sounds the Abrahamic promise that the seed would be as numberless as the sand; Paul ironically juxtaposes the vast promised multitude with the saved remnant.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.
echoes.note: The 'Sodom and Gomorrah' comparison cited in v.29 carries the figural weight of the destroyed cities of Genesis 19; the remnant 'seed' is what spares Israel from total annihilation like the cities of the plain.

echoes.text: Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldeans’ pride, will be like when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.
echoes.note: The Sodom/Gomorrah overthrow as a type of complete divine judgment (Isaiah 13:19, of Babylon) reinforces the destruction-imagery behind the Isaiah 1:9 quotation in v.29.

pericopes.text: What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith; but Israel, following after a law of righteousness, didn’t arrive at the law of righteousness. Why? Because they didn’t seek it by faith, but as it were by works of the law. They stumbled over the stumbling stone; even as it is written, “Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense; and no one who believes in him will be disappointed.”

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: v.33, formula-marked ('as it is written'): 'Behold, I lay in Zion... a stone... and no one who believes in him will be disappointed/put to shame' quotes Isaiah's cornerstone oracle. Paul fuses it with Isaiah 8:14 to make the laid stone both foundation and stumbling block.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
echoes.note: v.33 'a stumbling stone and a rock of offense' is quoted from Isaiah 8:14, where the LORD himself becomes 'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense' to both houses of Israel. Paul conflates it with 28:16 to explain why Israel stumbled while Gentiles attained righteousness by faith.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.
echoes.note: v.31-32 Israel 'pursuing/following after' a law of righteousness faintly echoes Isaiah's address to 'you who pursue righteousness, who seek the LORD,' inverted: Israel pursued by works, not faith, and so failed to attain it.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The stumbling-stone/Zion-stone complex of v.32-33 belongs to the broader 'stone' testimonia tradition that also includes 'the stone the builders rejected'; Paul's stone Christology participates in this cluster though he cites only the Isaiah texts here.

pericopes.text: Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God is for Israel, that they may be saved. For I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they didn’t subject themselves to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.
echoes.note: 'You who pursue righteousness, who seek the LORD' — the verb pair pursue/seek righteousness underlies Paul's diagnosis that Israel 'sought to establish their own righteousness.' Thematic resonance with Isaianic righteousness language but no verbal quotation; disputed.

echoes.text: Don’t say in your heart, after Yahweh your God has thrust them out from before you, saying, “For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in to possess this land”; because Yahweh drives them out before you because of the wickedness of these nations. Not for your righteousness, or for the uprightness of your heart, do you go in to possess their land; but for the wickedness of these nations Yahweh your God does drive them out from before you, and that he may […]
echoes.note: Moses warns Israel not to say 'in their heart' that their own righteousness has earned the land — the seed of the 'establish their own righteousness' motif. The 'do not say in your heart' formula recurs verbatim in 10:6, so its conceptual root here (self-righteousness vs. God's gift) is a plausible anticipatory echo.

echoes.text: “I am inquired of by those who didn’t ask; I am found by those who didn’t seek me: I said, See me, see me, to a nation that was not called by my name. I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts;
echoes.note: The chapter's terminal quotation (cited at 10:20-21) describes a people zealous yet disobedient; Israel's 'zeal for God but not according to knowledge' here anticipates that Isaianic portrait of a contrary people. Forward-pointing thematic echo binding the pericope to the chapter's close.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: telos/'end of the law' language; for Paul elsewhere love-of-neighbor is the law's fulfillment. Faint and disputed connection to the meaning of Christ as the law's goal; included for maximal coverage.

pericopes.text: For Moses writes about the righteousness of the law, “The one who does them will live by them.” But the righteousness which is of faith says this, “Don’t say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down); or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.)” But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth, and in your heart”; that is, the word of faith, which we preach: that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart, one believes unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in him will not be disappointed.” For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him. For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Formula-cited: 'Moses writes about the righteousness of the law' introduces 'The one who does them will live by them' — a near-verbatim quotation of Leviticus 18:5 ('which if a man do, he shall live in them'). Paul makes it the voice of law-righteousness over against faith-righteousness. Also quoted at Galatians 3:12; high recurrence in Paul.

echoes.text: It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.
echoes.note: Formula-introduced ('the righteousness of faith says'): 'Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven... Who will descend into the abyss... The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart' — a sustained verbatim quotation of Deuteronomy 30:12-14, reworked christologically (ascend = bring Christ down; descend into the abyss = bring Christ up from the dead). High volume, the structural backbone of the pericope.

echoes.text: Don’t say in your heart, after Yahweh your God has thrust them out from before you, saying, “For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in to possess this land”; because Yahweh drives them out before you because of the wickedness of these nations.
echoes.note: The opening 'Do not say in your heart' in 10:6 conflates Deuteronomy 30:12 with the warning formula of Deuteronomy 9:4 ('Do not say in your heart... my righteousness'), which directly concerns self-righteousness. Strong verbal borrowing that splices the anti-self-righteousness warning onto the faith-word quotation. Widely recognized double allusion.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant.
echoes.note: The immediately preceding verse — 'this commandment is not too hard for you, nor is it far off' — sets up the not-in-heaven/not-beyond-the-sea contrast Paul exploits. Borrowed context for the 'word is near' argument even though only vv.12-14 are quoted.

echoes.text: They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble.
echoes.note: 'They mount up to heaven, they go down to the depths (abyss)' — the heaven/abyss merism for cosmic extremity. Paul's pairing 'ascend into heaven / descend into the abyss' may draw on this stock idiom; Deut 30 itself says 'beyond the sea,' so the 'abyss' wording suggests a secondary scriptural idiom. Disputed.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: Formula-cited: 'the Scripture says, Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame/disappointed' — a quotation of Isaiah 28:16 (the precious cornerstone in Zion). Paul adds the universalizing 'whoever' (pas). Recurs at Romans 9:33, knitting chapters 9-10 together; high volume and recurrence.

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: Formula-cited climax: 'Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved' — verbatim quotation of Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5). Paul reads kyrios as the risen Jesus (10:9, 'Jesus is Lord'), grounding the Jew-Greek universalism of 10:12. Also cited in Acts 2:21; high recurrence.

echoes.text: But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.
echoes.note: The 'mouth... heart' pairing of the Deut quotation is redeployed by Paul in 10:9-10 (confess with the mouth, believe in the heart). This is an exegetical extension of the quoted text — Paul mines the very words 'mouth/heart' to structure confession and faith. Strong internal echo of the source just cited.

echoes.text: You will know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am Yahweh, your God, and there is no one else; and my people will never again be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'You shall... not be put to shame' in Joel 2:27, just before the quoted v.32, shares the not-ashamed motif Paul draws from Isaiah 28:16. Possible reinforcing echo from the Joel context Paul is already mining. Disputed.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: 'the abyss' (abyssos) as primeval deep; Paul's substitution of 'abyss' for Deut's 'beyond the sea' carries cosmic/death overtones (= realm of the dead, whence Christ is raised). Faint scriptural background for the abyss imagery. Disputed.

pericopes.text: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!” But they didn’t all listen to the glad news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?” So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. But I say, didn’t they hear? Yes, most certainly, “Their sound went out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.” But I ask, didn’t Israel know? First Moses says, “I will provoke you to jealousy with that which is no nation, with a nation void of understanding I will make you angry.” Isaiah is very bold, and says, “I was found by those who didn’t seek me. I was revealed to those who didn’t ask for me.” But as to Israel he says, “All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('as it is written'): 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things' — quotation of Isaiah 52:7 (the herald announcing 'Your God reigns'). Paul reads the herald's gospel of return-from-exile as the apostolic gospel. High volume; central to the chain on hearing/preaching.

echoes.text: Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.
echoes.note: 'Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings, who proclaims peace' — closely parallels Isaiah 52:7 and may be conflated in Paul's wording (feet + good tidings + peace). Possible secondary scriptural source for the same image. Disputed.

echoes.text: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?
echoes.note: Formula-cited: 'Isaiah says, Lord, who has believed our report?' — verbatim quotation of Isaiah 53:1, the opening of the Servant Song. Paul uses Israel's unbelief at the Servant's message to explain why 'they did not all heed the gospel.' The 'report' (akoe) is punningly tied to 'faith comes by hearing (akoe)' in 10:17. High volume and theological weight.

echoes.text: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?
echoes.note: Separate echo: 10:17 ('faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ') exploits the LXX term akoe ('report/what is heard') from the Isaiah 53:1 quotation just given. Paul's whole hearing→faith chain is generated by the double sense of akoe in the source text. Verbal-exegetical echo distinct from the bare quotation.

echoes.text: Their voice has gone out through all the earth, their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,
echoes.note: Formula-introduced rhetorically ('did they not hear? Yes...'): 'Their sound went out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world' — verbatim quotation of Psalm 19:4 (LXX 18:5). Paul transfers the cosmic witness of the heavens to the universal proclamation of the gospel, answering whether Israel has heard. High volume.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('First Moses says'): 'I will provoke you to jealousy with that which is no nation; with a nation void of understanding I will make you angry' — verbatim quotation of Deuteronomy 32:21 from the Song of Moses. Grounds Paul's jealousy motif (cf. 11:11,14): Gentile inclusion provokes Israel. High recurrence in Paul's argument across chs. 9-11.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: Beyond the quotation, the Song of Moses (Deut 32) as a whole — Israel's faithlessness, God's turn to a foolish nation, eventual mercy — supplies the deep structure of Romans 9-11. The 'no-people/no-understanding' framing echoes through Paul's Gentile argument. Recurrence-based echo of the broader source context.

echoes.text: “I am inquired of by those who didn’t ask; I am found by those who didn’t seek me: I said, See me, see me, to a nation that was not called by my name.
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('Isaiah is very bold and says'): 'I was found by those who did not seek me; I was revealed to those who did not ask for me' — quotation of Isaiah 65:1, applied to the Gentiles who found God without seeking. High volume; pairs antithetically with the next verse on Israel.

echoes.text: I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts;
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('But as to Israel he says'): 'All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people' — verbatim quotation of Isaiah 65:2, the chapter's climactic indictment of Israel's disobedience. Paired with 65:1 to contrast believing Gentiles and resistant Israel; high volume, the rhetorical capstone of ch. 10.

echoes.text: Why, when I came, was there no man? when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened at all, that it can’t redeem? or have I no power to deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a wilderness: their fish stink, because there is no water, and die for thirst.
echoes.note: 'Why, when I came, was there no one? ... Is my hand shortened?' — the motif of God's outstretched/extended hand meeting no response resonates with 'all day long I stretched out my hands.' Faint reinforcing Isaianic echo. Disputed.

echoes.text: The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge. There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard.
echoes.note: The fuller Psalm 19 context — the heavens declaring God's glory with speech that has 'no words... yet their voice goes out' — undergirds Paul's claim that the gospel proclamation reaches everyone. Background of the quoted v.4. Disputed as to intentional reach.

pericopes.text: I ask then, did God reject his people? May it never be! For I also am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God didn’t reject his people, which he foreknew. Or don’t you know what the Scripture says about Elijah? How he pleads with God against Israel: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have broken down your altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life.” But how does God answer him? “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work. What then? That which Israel seeks for, that he didn’t obtain, but the chosen ones obtained it, and the rest were hardened. According as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, to this very day.” David says, “Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, a stumbling block, and a retribution to them. Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see. Bow down their back always.”

echoes.text: For Yahweh won’t reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.
echoes.note: Paul's opening 'God did not reject his people' (v.1-2) verbally tracks the psalm's promise 'the LORD will not reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.' Same verb of rejection, same object 'his people'; it functions almost as an embedded near-quotation grounding the whole argument.

echoes.text: For Yahweh will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it has pleased Yahweh to make you a people to himself.
echoes.note: Samuel: 'the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.' Paul's denial of rejection draws on this covenant-fidelity formula; pairs with Ps 94:14 as the scriptural backbone of v.1-2 'God did not reject his people.'

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: Paul's self-identification as 'a descendant of Abraham' (v.1) leans on the Abrahamic covenant promise to the seed; faint, but it grounds his claim that membership in the people persists by descent and election.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Verbatim of Elijah's complaint at Horeb: 'they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they seek my life.' Paul cites it formulaically ('don't you know what the Scripture says about Elijah... how he pleads with God against Israel') to introduce the remnant theme (v.3).

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's complaint is repeated verbatim in 1 Kgs 19:14 (the second utterance to the LORD); Paul's v.3 reproduces this doubled lament. Listed separately because the source occurs at both v.10 and v.14 (recurrence within the source narrative).

echoes.text: Yet will I leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.”
echoes.note: Formula-cited divine answer (v.4): 'I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' Verbatim of the LORD's reply to Elijah; the foundational proof-text for Paul's doctrine of a preserved remnant 'according to the election of grace' (v.5).

echoes.text: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, in the midst of all the earth.
echoes.note: The remnant motif of v.5 ('a remnant according to the election of grace') draws on Isaiah's remnant theology ('though your people be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return'), a text Paul has already quoted in Rom 9:27-28. Strong conceptual borrowing of the 'remnant' (leimma/hypoleimma) word-field.

echoes.text: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('as it is written') in v.8: 'God gave them a spirit of stupor (pneuma katanyxeos)' is verbatim from Isa 29:10 LXX, 'the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep.' Supplies the head phrase of the conflated citation about Israel's hardening.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: The continuation of v.8 — 'eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear, to this very day' — is verbatim from Deut 29:4 ('the LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day'). Paul fuses it with Isa 29:10 into a single formula-introduced quotation; 'to this very day' is the Deuteronomy tag.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The 'eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear' hardening language of v.8 also resonates with Isaiah's commissioning oracle ('hearing you will hear and not understand; seeing you will see and not perceive'), the classic hardening text. Reinforces the conflated citation's theme even if Deut 29:4 supplies the closer wording.

echoes.text: Let their table before them become a snare. May it become a retribution and a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they can’t see. Let their backs be continually bent.
echoes.note: Attributed quotation (v.9-10, 'David says'): 'Let their table be made a snare and a trap... Let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bow down their back always.' Verbatim of Ps 69:22-23 LXX. A psalm of the righteous sufferer Paul reads imprecatorily against the hardened; pairs the 'darkened eyes' with the Isaiah/Deut citation of v.8.

echoes.text: Let destruction come on him unawares. Let his net that he has hidden catch himself. Let him fall into that destruction.
echoes.note: The 'snare/trap' imprecation of v.9 also echoes the wider psalmic curse tradition ('let destruction come upon him unawares, and let his net that he hid catch himself'). Faint reinforcement of the Ps 69 citation.

pericopes.text: I ask then, did they stumble that they might fall? May it never be! But by their fall salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy. Now if their fall is the riches of the world, and their loss the riches of the Gentiles; how much more their fullness? For I speak to you who are Gentiles. Since then as I am an apostle to Gentiles, I glorify my ministry; if by any means I may provoke to jealousy those who are my flesh, and may save some of them. For if the rejection of them is the reconciling of the world, what would their acceptance be, but life from the dead? If the first fruit is holy, so is the lump. If the root is holy, so are the branches. But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them, and became partaker with them of the root and of the richness of the olive tree; don’t boast over the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you. You will say then, “Branches were broken off, that I might be grafted in.” True; by their unbelief they were broken off, and you stand by your faith. Don’t be conceited, but fear; for if God didn’t spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. See then the goodness and severity of God. Toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off. They also, if they don’t continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut out of that which is by nature a wild olive tree, and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree, how much more will these, which are the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree?

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: 'to provoke them to jealousy' (v.11, again v.14) borrows directly from the Song of Moses: 'they have moved me to jealousy... I will provoke them to jealousy by those who are not a people.' Paul already quoted Deut 32:21 at Rom 10:19; here he deploys its key verb (parazeloo) as the engine of his Gentiles-to-Israel argument. Strong verbal borrowing with recurrence.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When you come into the land where I bring you, then it shall be that when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall offer up a wave offering to Yahweh. Of the first of your dough you shall offer up a cake for a wave offering. As the wave offering of the threshing floor, so you shall heave it. Of the first of your dough, you shall give to Yahweh a wave offering throughout […]
echoes.note: 'If the first fruit is holy, so is the lump' (v.16) draws on the dough/firstfruit offering of Num 15: a portion of the first of the dough (aparche) is given so the whole batch is sanctified. Paul applies the cultic logic of consecration-by-firstfruit to the patriarchs and Israel.

echoes.text: Yahweh called your name, A green olive tree, beautiful with goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he has kindled fire on it, and its branches are broken.
echoes.note: The olive-tree image for Israel (v.17-24, 'the root and the richness of the olive tree') borrows Jeremiah's figure: 'The LORD called your name, A green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit'—followed there by branches broken and burned for unbelief. Supplies both the olive-tree identification of Israel and the broken-branches judgment motif.

echoes.text: His branches will spread, and his beauty will be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon.
echoes.note: Hosea's restoration oracle pictures renewed Israel: 'his branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be like the olive tree.' Paul's olive-tree-with-spreading-branches and hope of regrafting (v.23-24) coheres with this restoration imagery alongside Jer 11:16.

echoes.text: But as for me, I am like a green olive tree in God’s house. I trust in God’s loving kindness forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'I am like a green olive tree in the house of God' — the righteous flourishing as an olive planted by God resonates faintly with Paul's cultivated 'good olive tree' (v.24) into which branches are grafted.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Don't boast over the branches... Don't be conceited, but fear' (v.18, 20) echoes 'Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and depart from evil.' The pairing of not-being-wise-in-self with fear is distinctive; recurs at v.25 ('wise in your own conceits').

echoes.text: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes' undergirds Paul's warning against Gentile conceit (v.18-20, 25). Faint thematic reinforcement of the Prov 3:7 admonition.

echoes.text: and the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’”
echoes.note: 'You stand by your faith' (v.20) faintly recalls Isaiah's word to Ahaz: 'If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established (stand firm).' The standing-by-faith / falling-by-unbelief antithesis coheres, though the verbal link is thin.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: 'Their acceptance... life from the dead' (v.15) reads Israel's future restoration typologically as resurrection, the figure of the valley of dry bones where dead Israel is raised and replanted in its land. Typological rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: For I don’t desire you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you won’t be wise in your own conceits, that a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved. Even as it is written, “There will come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob. This is my covenant to them, when I will take away their sins.” Concerning the Good News, they are enemies for your sake. But concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sake. For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For as you in time past were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy by their disobedience, even so these also have now been disobedient, that by the mercy shown to you they may also obtain mercy. For God has shut up all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all.

echoes.text: “A Redeemer will come to Zion, and to those who turn from disobedience in Jacob,” says Yahweh. “As for me, this is my covenant with them,” says Yahweh. “My Spirit who is on you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your seed, nor out of the mouth of your seed’s seed,” says Yahweh, “from henceforth and forever.”
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('as it is written') in v.26-27: 'There will come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.' Verbatim core from Isa 59:20-21 LXX ('the Deliverer will come for Zion's sake, and turn away ungodliness from Jacob'), with the 'covenant' clause flowing from 59:21. The backbone citation of the 'all Israel will be saved' climax.

echoes.text: Therefore by this the iniquity of Jacob will be forgiven, and this is all the fruit of taking away his sin: that he makes all the stones of the altar as chalk stones that are beaten in pieces, so that the Asherah poles and the incense altars shall rise no more.
echoes.note: 'This is my covenant to them, when I will take away their sins' (v.27b) supplies the sin-removal clause via Isa 27:9 LXX: 'this is his blessing, when I take away his sin.' Paul conflates it with Isa 59:20-21; the phrase 'take away their sins' is the Isa 27:9 contribution to the composite citation.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: and they shall teach no more every man his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know Yahweh; for they shall all know me, from their least to their greatest, says Yahweh: for I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin […]
echoes.note: 'This is my covenant to them, when I will take away their sins' (v.27) also draws the new-covenant formula from Jer 31:33-34 ('this is the covenant I will make... I will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more'). The 'covenant + forgiveness of sins' pairing is distinctively Jeremianic; Paul fuses it into the Isaianic Deliverer oracle.

echoes.text: Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'Out of Zion' as the source of deliverance (v.26) resonates with Zion-centered eschatology ('out of Zion shall go forth the law'). Faint thematic backdrop to the quoted Isa 59:20.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: 'A partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in' (v.25) sustains the Isaianic hardening motif of the chapter (cf. the Isa 29:10 citation at v.8). The temporal 'until' frames the hardening as the bounded judicial blindness of Isaiah's commission.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers' sake' (v.28) draws on Deuteronomy's election theology: 'because the LORD loved you... and because he would keep the oath which he swore to your fathers.' The love-of-Israel-for-the-fathers'-sake is the Deuteronomic ground Paul invokes.

echoes.text: Only Yahweh had a delight in your fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all peoples, as at this day.
echoes.note: 'The LORD had a delight in your fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them' directly undergirds v.28's 'beloved for the fathers' sake' and v.29's irrevocable calling. Pairs with Deut 7:7-8 as the election-of-the-patriarchs source.

echoes.text: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?
echoes.note: 'The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (v.29) coheres with Balaam's oracle that God 'is not a man, that he should lie... has he said, and will he not do it?'—the unchangeableness of God's word toward Israel. Faint thematic support.

pericopes.text: Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” “Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?” For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.

echoes.text: Who has directed the Spirit of Yahweh, or has taught him as his counselor?
echoes.note: Verbatim quotation (v.34): 'For who has known the mind of the LORD? Or who has been his counselor?' from Isa 40:13 LXX ('who has known the mind of the LORD, and who has been his counselor that he might instruct him?'). Caps the doxology on the unsearchability of God's wisdom.

echoes.text: Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Everything under the heavens is mine.
echoes.note: Quotation (v.35): 'Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?' rendering Job 41:11 ('who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is mine'). Paul follows a Hebrew-leaning form (the LXX differs), asserting God's unindebted sovereignty.

echoes.text: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways,” says Yahweh. “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
echoes.note: 'How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out' (v.33) borrows Isaiah's 'my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways... as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways.' The inscrutable 'ways' of God is the shared figure, and Isa 40-55 supplies the doxology's whole register.

echoes.text: who does great things that can’t be fathomed, marvelous things without number;
echoes.note: 'Who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number' resonates with v.33's 'unsearchable judgments... past tracing out.' Coheres with the Job-framed doxology that closes with the Job 41:11 citation.

echoes.text: He does great things past finding out; yes, marvelous things without number.
echoes.note: 'Who does great things past finding out, yes, marvelous things without number' parallels v.33's untraceable ways of God. Faint reinforcement of the Joban wisdom backdrop to the doxology.

echoes.text: Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself?
echoes.note: 'Have you heard the secret counsel of God?'—the rhetorical challenge to anyone claiming to be God's counselor—anticipates v.34's 'who has been his counselor?' alongside the primary Isa 40:13 quotation.

echoes.text: For what man will know the counsel of God? Or who will conceive what the Lord willeth?
echoes.note: 'For what man can know the counsel of God? Or who can conceive what the Lord wills?' (deuterocanonical) closely parallels v.34's question and likely stands in the same wisdom-doxology stream Paul draws on; some see it as a mediating source for the Isa 40:13 citation.

echoes.text: For who has stood in the council of Yahweh, that he should perceive and hear his word? who has marked my word, and heard it?
echoes.note: 'Who has stood in the council of the LORD, that he should perceive and hear his word?' faintly underlies v.34's 'who has been his counselor?'—the prophetic topos of no human admittance to the divine council.

pericopes.text: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

echoes.text: “‘If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without defect. He shall offer it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, that he may be accepted before Yahweh. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
echoes.note: "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God" reuses the technical cultic vocabulary of the burnt offering, which must be presented/brought 'acceptable before the LORD' (LXX dekton). Paul figurally transposes the Levitical offering from animal victim to the embodied self.

echoes.text: For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
echoes.note: The Psalm's claim that God does not delight in animal sacrifice but in 'a broken spirit' anticipates Paul's redefinition of true worship (logike latreia) as the offering of the whole self rather than the slain victim.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice' belongs to the prophetic stream that internalizes and ethicizes cult; Paul's 'reasonable/spiritual service' redirects sacrifice toward obedient self-presentation in the same key.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' is part of the prophetic critique that grounds Paul's reframing of worship as embodied, merciful obedience rather than ritual offering.

echoes.text: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: Micah's rhetorical rejection of burnt offerings in favor of doing justice and walking humbly parallels Paul's contrast between cultic sacrifice and 'living sacrifice' as the true service God requires.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The promise of a 'new heart and a new spirit' stands behind 'be transformed by the renewing of your mind'; the eschatological interior renewal of the prophets is here applied to the believing community.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant law written on the heart/mind (LXX dianoia) coheres with the 'renewing of the mind' that enables one to discern God's will; faint verbal contact via mind/heart-renewal.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Discerning and doing 'the good and acceptable and perfect will of God' echoes Deuteronomy's insistence that God's commandment is knowable and doable, internalized in heart and mouth — a theme Paul invokes nearby in Romans 10.

pericopes.text: For I say, through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith. For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another. Having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us, if prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of our faith; or service, let us give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching; or he who exhorts, to his exhorting: he who gives, let him do it with liberality; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Not to think of himself more highly than he ought' draws on the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes'; the same maxim returns explicitly at 12:16, framing the pericope's call to sober self-estimation.

echoes.text: Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
echoes.note: 'Do you see a man wise in his own conceit? There is more hope for a fool' supplies the proverbial backdrop for Paul's exhortation against inflated self-regard ('think reasonably').

echoes.text: Pride is hateful before the Lord and before men; And in the judgement of both will unrighteousness err.
echoes.note: Sirach's wisdom that 'pride is hateful before the Lord and before men' is a Second Temple parallel to Paul's call not to over-rate oneself but to measure by the faith God apportions.

pericopes.text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good. In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate one to another; in honor preferring one another; not lagging in diligence; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord; rejoicing in hope; enduring in troubles; continuing steadfastly in prayer; contributing to the needs of the saints; given to hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep. Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits. Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men. If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men. Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.” Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.” Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

echoes.text: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”
echoes.note: 12:19 cites with the formula 'it is written': 'Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.' The wording reflects the Song of Moses (with a form closer to the Targum/Hebrew than LXX), making divine retribution the ground for renouncing personal revenge.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: 12:20 quotes nearly verbatim: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so you will heap coals of fire on his head.' Paul takes over the LXX wisdom saying whole as the positive counterpart to renounced vengeance.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge... you shall love your neighbor' is the holiness-code substratum of the whole love-section: 'let love be without hypocrisy,' 'do not avenge yourselves,' and the love of brothers all draw on this command Paul elsewhere makes the summary of the law (13:9).

echoes.text: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”
echoes.note: 'Abhor that which is evil; cling to that which is good' (12:9) closely renders the prophetic imperative 'Hate evil and love good'; the antithetical evil/good pairing matches Amos's covenant ethics.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Depart from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it' underlies both 'abhor evil... cling to good' (12:9) and 'be at peace with all men' (12:18); the twin evil-shunning and peace-pursuing maxims are reflected together.

echoes.text: You who love Yahweh, hate evil. He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.
echoes.note: 'You who love the LORD, hate evil' offers a further scriptural pairing of love and abhorrence of evil behind 12:9.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Do not be wise in your own conceits' (12:16) reproduces 'Be not wise in your own eyes' (LXX), the same proverb that grounded 12:3; here it caps the call to humble association with the lowly.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes' reinforces the prophetic condemnation of self-conceit that Paul forbids in 12:16.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD and he will save you' is the wisdom source for 'Repay no one evil for evil' (12:17) joined to leaving wrath to God (12:19) — the Proverb already links non-retaliation with reliance on divine vindication.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done' directly parallels the prohibition of returning evil for evil in 12:17.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: 'Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men' (12:17) echoes 'find favor and good repute in the sight of God and man' (LXX Prov 3:4), the wisdom ideal of conduct visibly good before others.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' undergirds 'associate with the humble; do not be high-minded' (12:16); the humility motif is the same wisdom orientation James and 1 Peter also draw from this verse.

echoes.text: Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn.
echoes.note: 'Do not fail those who weep, but mourn with those who mourn' is a strikingly close Second Temple parallel to 'weep with those who weep' (12:15); a wisdom maxim of empathetic solidarity rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: Didn’t I weep for him who was in trouble? Wasn’t my soul grieved for the needy?
echoes.note: 'Did I not weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the poor?' anticipates the compassionate mourning-with-the-mourner of 12:15.

echoes.text: But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth. I afflicted my soul with fasting. My prayer returned into my own bosom. I behaved myself as though it had been my friend or my brother. I bowed down mourning, as one who mourns his mother.
echoes.note: The psalmist's mourning and prayer for his persecutors ('I afflicted myself... I went about as one who laments for his mother') parallels both 'weep with those who weep' (12:15) and 'bless those who persecute you' (12:14).

echoes.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: The command to love the resident alien 'as yourself' grounds the welcome of strangers behind 'given to hospitality' (12:13) within the same holiness-code love ethic that governs the pericope.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: Abraham's hospitality to the three visitors is the paradigm narrative of welcome that informs the early-Christian virtue 'given to hospitality' (12:13).

echoes.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord. For great is the potency of the Lord, And he is glorified of those who are lowly.
echoes.note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself... what is committed to you, attend to in humility' parallels 'do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble' (12:16) as Second Temple humility instruction.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you God to whom vengeance belongs, you God to whom vengeance belongs, shine out.
echoes.note: 'O LORD, God of vengeance' confirms that retribution belongs to God alone — the theological premise of 12:19 that Paul anchors in Deuteronomy 32:35; possible secondary resonance.

echoes.text: May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand shall not be on you.
echoes.note: David's refusal to harm Saul — 'May the LORD avenge me on you, but my hand shall not be against you' — is a narrative enactment of leaving vengeance to God and not repaying evil for evil (12:17, 19).

pericopes.text: Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God. Therefore he who resists the authority, withstands the ordinance of God; and those who withstand will receive to themselves judgment. For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Do you desire to have no fear of the authority? Do that which is good, and you will have praise from the same, for he is a servant of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid, for he doesn’t bear the sword in vain; for he is a servant of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Therefore you need to be in subjection, not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake. For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are servants of God’s service, attending continually on this very thing. Give therefore to everyone what you owe: taxes to whom taxes are due; customs to whom customs; respect to whom respect; honor to whom honor.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: Paul's axiom 'there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God' restates Daniel's hymn that God 'changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings.' Strong thematic and conceptual borrowing: the establishment and deposing of rulers is God's act, the theological ground for v.1.

echoes.text: The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones; to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.
echoes.note: 'The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will' (cf. 4:25, 4:32) is the Danielic doctrine that earthly dominion is conferred by God, directly underwriting 'ordained by God' and 'a servant of God.'

echoes.text: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. By me princes rule; nobles, and all the righteous rulers of the earth.
echoes.note: Wisdom declares 'By me kings reign, and rulers decree justice; by me princes rule.' The claim that legitimate rule derives from God and exists to commend the good (v.3) closely tracks this sapiential formula.

echoes.text: Hear therefore, you kings, and understand; Learn, you judges of the ends of the earth: Give ear, you that have dominion over much people, And make your boast in multitudes of nations. Because your dominion was given you from the Lord, And your sovereignty from the Most High; Who will search out your works, And will make inquisition of your counsels:
echoes.note: Address to rulers: 'your dominion was given you from the Lord, and your sovereignty from the Most High, who will search out your works.' This Second Temple text gives the nearest verbal-conceptual parallel to vv.1-4 (authority delegated by God; rulers accountable as God's ministers). Many read Romans 13 as engaging precisely this Hellenistic-Jewish political theology.

echoes.text: Because being officers of his kingdom you did not judge aright, Neither kept you law, nor walked after the counsel of God. Awfully and swiftly will he come upon you; Because a stern judgement befalleth those who are in high place:
echoes.note: Rulers are called 'servants/ministers of his kingdom' who will be judged for failing to govern rightly — parallel to Paul's repeated 'servant of God' (diakonos/leitourgos, vv.4,6) and the threat of wrath upon wrongdoers.

echoes.text: In the hand of the Lord is the authority of the earth; And in due time he will raise up over it one that is profitable.
echoes.note: 'The government of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and over it he will raise up the right leader for the time' — Ben Sira's statement that political authority and its incumbents are God-appointed coheres tightly with vv.1-2.

echoes.text: I have made the earth, the men and the animals that are on the surface of the earth, by my great power and by my outstretched arm; and I give it to whom it seems right to me. Now have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and the animals of the field also have I given him to serve him.
echoes.note: God: 'I have made the earth... and I give it to whomever it seems right to me. Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar... my servant.' A pagan king is called God's 'servant' and his rule is divinely ordained — striking precedent for calling the (Roman) ruler 'a servant of God' (vv.4,6).

echoes.text: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.
echoes.note: 'Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you... and pray to the LORD on its behalf' — the exilic posture of submission to and cooperation with a foreign government anticipates Paul's counsel of subjection, taxes, and honor (vv.5-7).

echoes.text: My son, fear Yahweh and the king. Don’t join those who are rebellious:
echoes.note: 'My son, fear the LORD and the king' pairs reverence for God with honor due the ruler — directly behind the closing exhortation to render 'respect to whom respect, honor to whom honor' (v.7).

echoes.text: I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God. Don’t be hasty to go out of his presence. Don’t persist in an evil thing, for he does whatever pleases him, for the king’s word is supreme. Who can say to him, “What are you doing?” Whoever keeps the commandment shall not come to harm, and his wise heart will know the time and procedure.
echoes.note: 'Keep the king's command... whoever keeps a command will not experience harm' — wisdom on prudent obedience to royal authority parallels Paul's 'be in subjection... do good and you will have praise' (vv.3-5).

echoes.text: “You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
echoes.note: 'You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people' — Torah pairs honoring God with not dishonoring the civil authority, an antecedent to 'he who resists the authority withstands the ordinance of God' (v.2) and 'honor to whom honor' (v.7).

echoes.text: Whoever sheds man’s blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image.
echoes.note: 'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed' — the foundational warrant for human authority to execute lethal justice stands behind 'he does not bear the sword in vain... an avenger for wrath' (v.4).

echoes.text: But God is the judge. He puts down one, and lifts up another.
echoes.note: 'It is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another' — God's sovereignty over the rise and fall of rulers undergirds 'those who exist are ordained by God' (v.1).

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all; and in your hand is power and might; and it is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all.
echoes.note: David's doxology: 'Yours is the kingdom, O LORD... power and might are in your hand.' The conviction that all rule belongs to and flows from God is the broader scriptural matrix for vv.1-2.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held, to subdue nations before him, and strip kings of their armor; to open the doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut:
echoes.note: God names the Persian Cyrus 'his anointed' and uses a pagan emperor as instrument of his purposes — a figural precedent for treating the Roman magistrate as 'God's servant' (vv.4,6) without the ruler's knowledge of God.

pericopes.text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: Verbatim citation of the second-table Decalogue commandments: 'You shall not commit adultery,' 'You shall not murder,' 'You shall not steal,' 'You shall not covet.' Paul lists adultery before murder, following the Septuagint order of Deuteronomy 5 (and Exodus 20 LXX manuscripts).

echoes.text: “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. Neither shall you desire your neighbor’s house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.”
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic recension of the same commandments; the LXX of Deuteronomy 5 places adultery before murder, matching Paul's sequence in v.9, so this is the likely proximate text.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Explicit verbatim quotation: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' which Paul names as the saying in which all the commandments are 'summed up.' The interpretive move (love of neighbor as the epitome of the law) recurs in Romans (cf. 13:10) and Galatians 5:14.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: v.10 'Love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law' continues to expound the same Levitical command, drawing out its negative corollary as the substance of all the prohibitions just cited.

pericopes.text: Do this, knowing the time, that it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep, for salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed. The night is far gone, and the day is near. Let’s therefore throw off the works of darkness, and let’s put on the armor of light. Let us walk properly, as in the day; not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.
