echoes.text: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.
echoes.note: 'He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head' — the divine-warrior imagery of donning protective armor underlies 'put on the armor of light' (v.12) and 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (v.14). Paul develops this same Isaianic armor motif at Ephesians 6 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8.

echoes.text: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet; He will take holiness as an invincible shield,
echoes.note: 'He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, and wear impartial justice as a helmet' — this Second Temple reworking of Isaiah 59:17 stands in the same stream feeding Paul's 'put on the armor of light' (v.12).

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'Arise, shine, for your light has come... darkness shall cover the earth... but the LORD will arise upon you' — the dawning of eschatological light dispelling darkness parallels 'the night is far gone, the day is near' and the light/darkness antithesis of vv.12-13.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, put on your strength, Zion; put on your beautiful garments, Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean.
echoes.note: 'Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments' — combines the summons to wake and the imperative to 'put on,' both present in Paul's 'awaken out of sleep' (v.11) and 'put on the armor of light' / 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (vv.12,14).

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: 'Rouse yourself, rouse yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem' — the prophetic call to awaken to the hour of salvation parallels 'it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep' (v.11).

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' — the night-to-day, darkness-to-light reversal of vv.12-13 resonates with this classic salvation-light oracle.

echoes.text: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
echoes.note: 'He has clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decks himself' — the salvific 'putting on' of clothing as a figure for new status anticipates 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (v.14).

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' — the dawning day of salvation coheres with 'the day is near' (v.12) and the nearness of salvation (v.11).

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust' — eschatological awakening from sleep/death as a figure of salvation faintly parallels 'awaken out of sleep' (v.11).

echoes.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]
echoes.note: Those who 'rebel against the light' and work evil under cover of night/darkness anticipate 'the works of darkness' (v.12) contrasted with walking properly 'as in the day' (v.13).

echoes.text: Don’t be among ones drinking too much wine, or those who gorge themselves on meat: for the drunkard and the glutton shall become poor; and drowsiness clothes them in rags.
echoes.note: 'Be not among drunkards... for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty' — sapiential warning against carousing and drunkenness behind 'not in reveling and drunkenness' (v.13).

echoes.text: Woe to those who rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; who stay late into the night, until wine inflames them!
echoes.note: Woe to those who 'run after strong drink... till wine inflames them' — prophetic censure of revelry and drunkenness parallels the vice-list of v.13.

pericopes.text: Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions. One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables. Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him. Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand. One man esteems one day as more important. Another esteems every day alike. Let each man be fully assured in his own mind. He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks. He who doesn’t eat, to the Lord he doesn’t eat, and gives God thanks. For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written, “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘to me every knee will bow. Every tongue will confess to God.’” So then each one of us will give account of himself to God.

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: Paul's explicit formula-citation in 14:11 ('it is written, As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee will bow, every tongue will confess to God') quotes Isaiah 45:23 LXX. In Isaiah the universal bowing and swearing/confessing is rendered to YHWH alone as the only God and Savior; Paul deploys it to ground the certainty of universal accountability at the divine judgment seat. The same verse recurs at Philippians 2:10-11, showing Pauline thematic recurrence.

echoes.text: but in very deed, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with Yahweh’s glory;
echoes.note: The introductory divine-oath formula 'As I live, says the Lord' (zōn egō legei kyrios) prefixed to the Isaiah 45 quotation is not in Isaiah 45:23 itself; it is the LXX oath formula 'as I live' (ζῶ ἐγώ) characteristic of Numbers 14:21,28 and Ezekiel. Paul (or his Vorlage) conflates the oath formula with the Isaiah quotation to heighten its solemnity as a guarantee of universal judgment.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes all around, and see: all these gather themselves together, and come to you. As I live,” says Yahweh, “you shall surely clothe yourself with them all as with an ornament, and dress yourself with them, like a bride.
echoes.note: An alternative/complementary source for the prefixed oath 'As I live, says the Lord': Isaiah 49:18 ('As I live, says the LORD') stands within the same section of Isaiah as 45:23, making it a plausible internal-Isaianic source for the conflated formula rather than the Numbers/Ezekiel oath stock.

echoes.text: Therefore as I live, says the Lord Yahweh, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things, and with all your abominations, therefore will I also diminish you; neither shall my eye spare, and I also will have no pity.
echoes.note: Ezekiel is the densest concentration of the 'As I live, says the Lord' oath (Ezekiel 5:11; 14:16; 16:48; 33:11, etc.). The recurrence of the formula there may stand behind the LXX phrasing Paul attaches to the Isaiah citation; faint and not pointed to a single verse.

echoes.text: God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
echoes.note: The 'weak' eating only vegetables (lachana, 14:2) recalls the original Edenic vegetarian diet granted to humanity (Genesis 1:29, every seed-bearing plant for food). The contrast of vegetable-only vs. eating-all-things may evoke the pre-Noahic dietary order; thematic and faint, not verbal.

echoes.text: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.
echoes.note: The position that 'one has faith to eat all things' (panta phagein, 14:2) echoes the post-flood Noahic grant: 'Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as the green plants I gave you everything' (Genesis 9:3). Paul's 'all things are clean' (14:14,20) presupposes this universal grant of food over against later dietary restriction.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: The clean/unclean food dispute underlying 14:1-12 (and explicit in 14:14,20, 'nothing is unclean of itself... all things indeed are clean') directly engages the Levitical purity code distinguishing clean from unclean animals (Leviticus 11; cf. Deuteronomy 14). The 'weak' likely keep these distinctions; Paul's verdict that nothing is koinon in itself overturns the categorical force of Leviticus 11 for those in Christ.

echoes.text: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's parallel dietary legislation ('You shall not eat any abominable thing') reinforces the Levitical clean/unclean backdrop to the eating dispute. The 'weak in faith' who eat only vegetables may be observing scruples derived from this Torah food law (and/or avoiding marketplace meat of uncertain provenance).

echoes.text: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. Now God made Daniel to find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs. The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse […]
echoes.note: Daniel and his companions refuse the king's rich food and wine, eating only vegetables (LXX lachana / ospria) and water to avoid defilement (Daniel 1:12,16). This is the closest Scriptural antecedent to a diaspora Jew eating 'only vegetables' (14:2) out of purity scruple in a Gentile environment, providing a likely model for the 'weak.'

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Paul's axiom 'none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself... we are the Lord's' (14:7-8) reflects the creational logic that life is a gift wholly owed to its Giver (cf. Genesis 2:7, the breath of life from God). Faint thematic resonance of creaturely belonging rather than verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: 'We are the Lord's' (tou kyriou esmen, 14:8) echoes the creational ownership confessed in Psalm 24:1 ('The earth is the LORD's and its fullness'), which Paul cites elsewhere at 1 Corinthians 10:26 in a closely parallel food-and-conscience argument. The lordship grounding here is conceptually linked though not quoted.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: 'Each one of us will give account of himself to God' (14:12) coheres with the Wisdom expectation that 'God will bring every deed into judgment' (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Thematic accountability before the divine Judge; faint and conceptual.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: The motif of individual rendering of account to God who judges (14:10,12) resonates with Psalm 62:12 ('you will render to each according to his work'), a verse Paul invokes for judgment-according-to-works at Romans 2:6. The shared judgment-recompense logic links the chapters.

echoes.text: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?
echoes.note: 'We will all stand before the judgment seat of God/Christ' (14:10) carries the prophetic Day-of-the-LORD note of standing before the dread Judge (cf. Joel 2:11, 'who can endure it?'), reframed by Paul christologically. Very faint thematic echo.

pericopes.text: Therefore let’s not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling. I know, and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean of itself; except that to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean. Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died. Then don’t let your good be slandered, for the Kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then, let us follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up. Don’t overthrow God’s work for food’s sake. All things indeed are clean, however it is evil for that man who creates a stumbling block by eating. It is good to not eat meat, drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother stumbles, is offended, or is made weak. Do you have faith? Have it to yourself before God. Happy is he who doesn’t judge himself in that which he approves. But he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because it isn’t of faith; and whatever is not of faith is sin. Now to him who is able to establish you according to my Good News and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery which has been kept secret through long ages, but now is revealed, and by the Scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the eternal God, is made known for obedience of faith to all the nations; to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever! Amen.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: Paul's declaration 'nothing is unclean of itself... all things indeed are clean' (14:14,20) directly engages and relativizes the Levitical clean/unclean food code (Leviticus 11). The very term koinon ('common/unclean') is the purity vocabulary of the dietary law; Paul affirms the law's categories exist only for the one who reckons a thing unclean.

echoes.text: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.
echoes.note: 'All things indeed are clean' (panta kathara, 14:20) restates the universal Noahic food grant (Genesis 9:3, everything that lives given as food). Paul grounds Christian liberty regarding food in the creation/Noahic order that precedes and outranks the Levitical restriction.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The command not to 'put a stumbling block in his brother's way' (proskomma, 14:13) draws on the Holiness Code prohibition: 'You shall not put a stumbling block before the blind' (Leviticus 19:14 LXX, proskomma / skandalon). Paul transposes the literal physical stumbling-block into the moral injury of causing a fellow believer to fall.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'If your brother is grieved because of food, you walk no longer in love' (14:15) applies the love-of-neighbor command (Leviticus 19:18) that Paul has just made the fulfillment of the law in 13:8-10. The 'brother' (adelphos) language and the priority of love over one's own right enact Leviticus 19:18 directly.

echoes.text: “Now therefore, what do I do here,” says Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them mock,” says Yahweh, “and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.
echoes.note: 'Don't let your good be slandered/blasphemed' (mē blasphēmeisthō, 14:16) echoes the prophetic concern that God's name/people be 'blasphemed among the nations' (Isaiah 52:5 LXX), a verse Paul cites at Romans 2:24. The fear that the gospel-given 'good' becomes an occasion of blasphemy reuses this prophetic anxiety.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Let us follow after things which make for peace' (ta tēs eirēnēs diōkōmen, 14:19) closely echoes Psalm 34:14 LXX ('seek peace and pursue it,' zētēson eirēnēn kai diōxon autēn). The verb 'pursue' (diōkō) with 'peace' as object is the distinctive shared phrasing.

echoes.text: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
echoes.note: The build-up vs. tear-down language ('build one another up,' 14:19; 'don't overthrow God's work,' 14:20, katalye) resonates with the Jeremianic commission to 'pluck up and break down... to build and to plant' (Jeremiah 1:10). The oikodomē/kataluō opposition is a recurring prophetic idiom for God's constructive work among his people.

echoes.text: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.
echoes.note: 'The Kingdom of God is... righteousness, peace, and joy' (14:17) coheres with the prophetic vision that 'the work of righteousness shall be peace' (Isaiah 32:17), where dikaiosynē and eirēnē are paired as the fruit of the Spirit poured out (32:15). Thematic resonance of the Spirit-wrought eschatological order.

echoes.text: For you shall go out with joy, and be led out with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break out before you into singing; and all the trees of the fields shall clap their hands.
echoes.note: The triad 'peace and joy' as marks of the inbreaking Kingdom (14:17) faintly echoes the Isaianic new-exodus promise 'you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace' (Isaiah 55:12), where joy and peace characterize redeemed life under God's reign. Faint thematic.

echoes.text: Don’t look at the wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly.
echoes.note: 'It is good not to eat meat, drink wine...' (14:21) — the renunciation of wine for the sake of another — has a faint sapiential backdrop in wisdom warnings about wine (Proverbs 23:31, 'do not look at wine when it is red'). Here, however, abstinence is for the brother's sake, not self-discipline; the link is thematic and weak.

echoes.text: Show not yourself valiant in wine; For wine has destroyed many. The furnace proves the temper of steel by dipping; So does wine prove hearts in the quarreling of the proud. Wine is as good as life to men, If you drink it in its measure: What life is there to a man that is without wine? And it has been created to make men glad. Wine drunk in season and to satisfy Is joy of heart, and gladness of soul: Wine drunk largely is bitterness of soul, With […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's measured counsel on wine and food at table (Sirach 31:25-31), weighing one's conduct for the sake of fellow diners, offers a Second Temple sapiential parallel to Paul's 'it is good not to eat meat or drink wine' where another stumbles (14:21). Conceptual, not verbal.

echoes.text: Go your way—eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.
echoes.note: The blessing 'Happy is he who doesn't judge himself in that which he approves' (14:22) faintly resonates with the Qoheleth beatitude on eating one's bread and drinking one's wine with a clear conscience before God (Ecclesiastes 9:7, 'God has already approved your works'). Thematic resonance of approved, untroubled enjoyment.

echoes.text: But you, being sovereign over your strength, judge in gentleness, And with great forbearance do you govern us; For the power is your whenever you have the will. But you did teach your people by such works as these, How that the righteous must be a lover of men; And you did make your sons to be of good hope, Because you give repentance when men have sinned.
echoes.note: The doxological coda (14:23 long ending in WEB) celebrating 'the only wise God' (monō sophō theō) coheres with the Wisdom of Solomon's portrait of God's singular wisdom governing all (Wisdom of Solomon 12:18-19, cf. 7:24-27). Faint and tied to a textually disputed doxology often printed at 16:25-27.

pericopes.text: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up. For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.” For whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through patience and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. Now the God of patience and of encouragement grant you to be of the same mind one with another according to Christ Jesus, that with one accord you may with one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

echoes.text: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
echoes.note: Verbatim, formula-introduced ('as it is written'): 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me' = LXX Psalm 68:10b. Paul reads the psalm's righteous sufferer as Christ, with 'you' = God; the reproaches aimed at God land on Christ, grounding the call not to please oneself. High volume (exact wording) and strong recurrence in early Christian passion exegesis.

echoes.text: For the zeal of your house consumes me. The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
echoes.note: Beyond the verbatim citation, Paul reads the whole psalm typologically: the persecuted righteous one of Psalm 69 prefigures Christ. The same psalm is mined elsewhere in the NT passion narrative (zeal for your house, gall and vinegar) and by Paul at Romans 11:9-10, marking it a recurring messianic testimonium.

echoes.text: Sing to Yahweh a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand, and his holy arm, have worked salvation for him.
echoes.note: 'Sing to your name'/glorify-with-one-mouth language (15:6) and the catena's Gentile-praise theme that follows resonates with the Psalter's call to sing a new song before the nations; faint and thematic, anticipatory of the 15:9-12 chain.

pericopes.text: Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God. Now I say that Christ has been made a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, that he might confirm the promises given to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore will I give praise to you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.” Again he says, “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.” Again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles! Let all the peoples praise him.” Again, Isaiah says, “There will be the root of Jesse, he who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.” Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope, in the power of the Holy Spirit.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: 15:8: Christ became a servant of the circumcision 'to confirm the promises given to the fathers.' The patriarchal promises (Genesis 12:3; 17:4-7; 22:18) — that in Abraham all nations would be blessed — are the substrate; the Gentile-inclusion catena is presented as their fulfillment. Conceptual allusion rather than verbal.

echoes.text: You will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.
echoes.note: 15:8-9 pairs 'truth of God' (to the circumcision) with 'mercy' (to the Gentiles). The truth/mercy (emeth/chesed) word-pair toward the fathers echoes covenantal formulae like Micah 7:20 and Psalm 98:3; faint and diffuse.

echoes.text: Therefore I will give thanks to you, Yahweh, among the nations, and will sing praises to your name.
echoes.note: First link of the catena (15:9), formula-introduced ('As it is written'): 'I will give praise to you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name' = LXX Psalm 17:50. The Davidic king praises God among the nations; Paul reads the messianic David as drawing Gentiles into doxology. Verbatim agreement with LXX.

echoes.text: Therefore I will give thanks to you, Yahweh, among the nations, and will sing praises to your name.
echoes.note: Parallel form of the same citation (15:9): 2 Samuel 22:50 = Psalm 18:49 are the doublet of David's victory song. The Davidic frame is load-bearing for Paul's catena — Christ as the Davidic Messiah whose praise extends to the Gentiles (cf. 15:12, root of Jesse). Given its own entry because the doublet reinforces the Davidic key of the whole chain.

echoes.text: Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
echoes.note: Second link (15:10), formula-introduced ('Again he says'): 'Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.' Follows the longer LXX/Qumran (4QDeut) text of the Song of Moses, where the nations are summoned to rejoice WITH Israel — exactly the with-his-people inclusion Paul needs. High volume; the Song of Moses is a recurring witness to the nations' destiny.
echoes.lxxText: Rejoice, ye heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice ye Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward them that hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.

echoes.text: Praise Yahweh, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!
echoes.note: Third link (15:11), formula-introduced ('Again'): 'Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles! Let all the peoples praise him' = LXX Psalm 116:1. The shortest psalm, an unambiguous summons to the Gentiles to praise YHWH; verbatim LXX. Caps the doxological progression of the chain (praise among / rejoice with / praise by the Gentiles).

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse, who stands as a banner of the peoples; and his resting place will be glorious.
echoes.note: Fourth link and climax (15:12), formula-introduced ('Again, Isaiah says'): 'There will be the root of Jesse, he who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope' = LXX Isaiah 11:10. The LXX ('rule over' and 'hope in') diverges from the MT ('stand as a banner... seek') and Paul follows the LXX, which supplies both Gentile rule and Gentile hope, tying back to 15:13 'God of hope.' Davidic-messianic capstone of the catena.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: The 'root of Jesse' image (15:12) draws on the opening of the same oracle, Isaiah 11:1 (a shoot from the stump of Jesse, a branch from his roots). The whole shoot-of-Jesse messianic complex stands behind the quotation; verbal overlap in 'root/Jesse' makes it a strong allusion supporting the citation.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse, who stands as a banner of the peoples; and his resting place will be glorious.
echoes.note: 15:13 'the God of HOPE fill you... that you may abound in HOPE' verbally picks up the catchword from the just-cited Isaiah 11:10 LXX ('in him the Gentiles will hope'). Paul's benediction is keyed to the final quotation, knitting citation and prayer together — a deliberate gezerah-shawah on 'hope.'

pericopes.text: I myself am also persuaded about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish others. But I write the more boldly to you in part, as reminding you, because of the grace that was given to me by God, that I should be a servant of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving as a priest the Good News of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be made acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. I have therefore my boasting in Christ Jesus in things pertaining to God. For I will not dare to speak of any things except those which Christ worked through me, for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of God’s Spirit; so that from Jerusalem, and around as far as to Illyricum, I have fully preached the Good News of Christ; yes, making it my aim to preach the Good News, not where Christ was already named, that I might not build on another’s foundation. But, as it is written, “They will see, to whom no news of him came. They who haven’t heard will understand.” Therefore also I was hindered these many times from coming to you, but now, no longer having any place in these regions, and having these many years a longing to come to you, whenever I journey to Spain, I will come to you. For I hope to see you on my journey, and to be helped on my way there by you, if first I may enjoy your company for a while. But now, I say, I am going to Jerusalem, serving the saints. For it has been the good pleasure of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem. Yes, it has been their good pleasure, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to serve them in fleshly things. When therefore I have accomplished this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will go on by way of you to Spain. I know that, when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of the Good News of Christ. Now I beg you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the love of the Spirit, that you strive together with me in your prayers to God for me, that I may be delivered from those who are disobedient in Judea, and that my service which I have for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints; that I may come to you in joy through the will of God, and together with you, find rest. Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

echoes.text: They shall bring all your brothers out of all the nations for an offering to Yahweh, on horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and on mules, and on dromedaries, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says Yahweh, as the children of Israel bring their offering in a clean vessel into Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 15:16: Paul is a 'leitourgos'/priest of the gospel 'that the offering up of the Gentiles might be made acceptable, sanctified.' Strong conceptual and lexical borrowing from Isaiah 66:19-20, where survivors are sent to the nations and the nations are brought 'as an offering to the LORD' to Jerusalem. Paul casts his Gentile mission as the eschatological priestly presentation of the nations.

echoes.text: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The 'acceptable offering' of/among the Gentiles (15:16) resonates with Malachi 1:11, where a pure offering is made to God's name 'among the nations.' Cultic-offering-among-Gentiles imagery; thematic with some lexical overlap (offering, acceptable, nations).

echoes.text: “I will set a sign among them, and I will send such as escape of them to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the islands afar off, who have not heard my fame, neither have seen my glory; and they shall declare my glory among the nations.
echoes.note: 15:19's geographic sweep ('from Jerusalem... as far as Illyricum, I have fully preached the gospel') and the 'signs' motif echo Isaiah 66:19, where God sets a sign and sends survivors to far coastlands/nations that have not heard or seen his glory — a program Paul sees himself enacting. Reinforced by the Isaiah 52:15 citation two verses later.

echoes.text: so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they understand.
echoes.note: 15:21, formula-introduced ('as it is written'): 'They will see, to whom no news of him came; they who haven't heard will understand' = LXX Isaiah 52:15. Drawn from the fourth Servant Song; Paul grounds his pioneer policy (not building on another's foundation) in the Servant's mission to those never told. Verbatim LXX.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high. Like as many were astonished at you (his appearance was marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men), so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they understand. Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of […]
echoes.note: By citing Isaiah 52:15 Paul reads his own apostolic mission figurally through the Suffering Servant: the Servant who startles many nations and whose report reaches those who had not heard becomes the template for the apostle to the Gentiles. Typological extension of the quotation into the broader Servant Song.

echoes.text: Then you shall see and be radiant, and your heart shall thrill and be enlarged; because the abundance of the sea shall be turned to you, the wealth of the nations shall come to you. The multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all they from Sheba shall come; they shall bring gold and frankincense, and shall proclaim the praises of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 15:25-27: the Gentile churches share their 'fleshly things' with Jerusalem because they partook of its 'spiritual things' — the collection. This evokes the prophetic vision of the nations bringing their wealth to Zion (Isaiah 60:5-6, 11; 66:12). Faint, thematic; Paul nowhere cites it, but the eschatological pilgrimage-of-the-nations pattern underlies the collection.

echoes.text: Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: 15:33 'the God of peace be with you all' draws on the Old Testament benedictory peace formula (Aaronic blessing, Numbers 6:26; cf. Judges 6:24 'the LORD is peace'). A liturgical echo rather than a citation; faint and formulaic.

pericopes.text: I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae, that you receive her in the Lord, in a way worthy of the saints, and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self. Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who for my life, laid down their own necks; to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles. Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ. Greet Mary, who labored much for us. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me. Greet Amplias, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved. Greet Apelles, the approved in Christ. Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet them of the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored much in the Lord. Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. The assemblies of Christ greet you.

echoes.text: The first of the first fruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
echoes.note: Epaenetus is called 'the first fruits (aparche) of Achaia.' The metaphor draws on the cultic offering of firstfruits — the first and best of the harvest consecrated to God (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:1-11). The link is purely conceptual reuse of an offering-term as a name for the first convert; no verbal borrowing, so faint and disputed.

pericopes.text: Now I beg you, brothers, look out for those who are causing the divisions and occasions of stumbling, contrary to the doctrine which you learned, and turn away from them. For those who are such don’t serve our Lord, Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by their smooth and flattering speech, they deceive the hearts of the innocent. For your obedience has become known to all. I rejoice therefore over you. But I desire to have you wise in that which is good, but innocent in that which is evil. And the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'The God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet' (16:20) alludes to the protoevangelium: 'he shall bruise/crush your head' addressed to the serpent. The verb (crush/bruise) plus the bodily image (head/feet, enemy trodden underfoot) reactivates Genesis 3:15, with Satan now read as the serpent and the church as the seed of the woman who treads him down. Strong verbal and figural coherence; Paul universalizes the promised victory.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: The image of the enemy placed 'under your feet' overlaps with the subjugation language of Psalm 8:6 ('you have put all things under his feet'), which Paul uses elsewhere for Christ's triumph. Here the dominant source is Genesis 3:15; the 'under feet' phrasing is at most a secondary, disputed resonance.

echoes.text: Everyone lies to his neighbor. They speak with flattering lips, and with a double heart. May Yahweh cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that boasts,
echoes.note: The dividers' 'smooth and flattering speech' that 'deceive the hearts of the innocent' (16:18) echoes the wisdom/psalmic indictment of smooth, flattering lips that deceive (Psalm 12:2-3; cf. Proverbs 26:28). Thematic and partly verbal but a common topos, so contested.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: The deceivers who beguile 'the hearts of the innocent' with smooth speech (16:18) typologically recall the serpent who deceived by crafty words — a figure reinforced two verses later by the explicit Genesis 3:15 allusion (16:20). The serpent-as-deceiver framing is suggestive but disputed as an intended echo here.

pericopes.text: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my relatives. I, Tertius, who write the letter, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, my host and host of the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the treasurer of the city, greets you, as does Quartus, the brother.
